title: From one living being to the whole Earth: how the levels of life depend on each other

summary.text: The air of Mars and Venus is almost all carbon dioxide, but one fifth of Earth's air is oxygen, and nearly all of it was made by living beings. In this unit you will run a paper planet of dark and pale daisies, and test whether a dark cloth gets warmer in sunlight.
summary.art: Three planets in a row seen from space, Venus cloudy yellow, the Earth blue and green, Mars red, with a small bar under each showing what its air is made of.

intro.hook: Take one slow breath in. About one fifth of the air you just took in is oxygen. Who made that oxygen, and where? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: Most people answer 'the trees near my home'. That is only a small part of the answer. The oxygen in your breath was made over a very long time by green plants, by seaweeds and by tiny green cells who float in the sea. So one breath joins you to living beings far away, and to living beings from long ago. In this unit you find out how one living being depends on the whole living Earth. You also test whether living beings can keep a planet steady.
intro.art: A child at an open window taking a breath, with faint lines leading from the breath to a tree, to the sea and to a tiny green cell.

outcomes: By the end I can name the five levels of life in order, and give an example of each.
By the end I can explain how a living being depends on the levels above them, and how each level is made by the beings in it.
By the end I can explain what an emergent property is, and give an example.
By the end I can tell balancing feedback from reinforcing feedback.
By the end I can give evidence that living beings have changed the Earth's air, soil, rain and temperature.
By the end I can say what the Daisy Planet model shows, and what a model cannot prove.
By the end I can explain the Gaia idea, give two criticisms of it, and say what is agreed and what is still argued about.

terms.meaning: An organism is one living being. A crow, a neem tree, a mushroom, a bacterium and you are each one organism.
terms.example: The crow on your window ledge is one organism.
terms.art: One house crow standing on a window ledge.

terms.meaning: A species is one kind of living being. Members of a species can have young together, and their young can have young too.
terms.example: All house crows are one species. Jungle crows are a different species.
terms.art: A house crow with a grey neck beside an all-black jungle crow.

terms.meaning: A population is all the members of one species who live in one place.
terms.example: All the house crows of Mylapore in Chennai are one population.
terms.art: Many house crows on the wires and roofs of one street.

terms.meaning: A community is all the populations of every species who live in one place. It includes the plants, animals, fungi and microbes.
terms.example: The crows, mynas, squirrels, neem trees, ants and soil bacteria of one street are a community.
terms.art: A street tree with crows, mynas, a squirrel and ants, and a magnified circle showing soil bacteria.

terms.meaning: An ecosystem is a community together with the non-living things around them. The non-living things are the water, air, soil, rock, sunlight and warmth.
terms.example: A temple tank is an ecosystem. It has fish, frogs, water plants and microbes, and also water, mud, air and sunlight.
terms.art: A stone temple tank with fish, lotus plants and a frog, with labels for the water, the mud and the sunlight.

terms.meaning: The biosphere is the part of the Earth where living beings are found. It is all the ecosystems of the Earth taken together.
terms.example: The deep sea, the Thar desert, a paddy field in Thanjavur and the air where a vulture flies are all parts of the biosphere.
terms.art: The Earth seen from space with a thin green and blue layer drawn around it.

terms.meaning: The atmosphere is the layer of air around a planet.
terms.example: The Earth's atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. The atmosphere of Mars is mostly carbon dioxide.
terms.art: A thin blue band of air around the curved edge of the Earth.

terms.meaning: A system is a set of parts that affect each other. Because the parts affect each other, a change in one part changes the others.
terms.example: A cycle is a system. The pedals turn the chain, the chain turns the wheel, and the brake slows the wheel.
terms.art: A bicycle with small arrows from the pedal to the chain to the back wheel.

terms.meaning: An emergent property is a feature that a whole has, and that none of its parts has alone.
terms.example: A heap of rice has a slope. One grain of rice has no slope.
terms.art: A cone-shaped heap of rice on a steel plate beside a single grain.

terms.meaning: Feedback happens when the result of a change comes back round and affects that same change.
terms.example: You feel hot, so you sweat. The sweat cools you, so you sweat less. The result came back and changed what started it.
terms.art: A circle of two arrows joining a hot face and a drop of sweat.

terms.meaning: Balancing feedback works against a change and brings things back towards where they were. Scientists also call it negative feedback. Here 'negative' means 'against the change'. It does not mean 'bad'.
terms.example: When the room gets warm, an air-conditioner with a thermostat cools it. When the room gets cold, the cooling stops.
terms.art: A see-saw coming back to level, with a small arrow pushing against the tilt.

terms.meaning: Reinforcing feedback adds to a change, so the change grows bigger and bigger. Scientists also call it positive feedback. Here 'positive' means 'adds to the change'. It does not mean 'good'.
terms.example: When white ice melts, dark sea is left. Dark sea takes in more sunlight, so the place warms and more ice melts.
terms.art: A patch of white sea ice breaking up, with dark water between the pieces and sun rays going into the water.

terms.meaning: Homeostasis means keeping conditions inside steady while conditions outside change.
terms.example: Your body stays close to 37 degrees Celsius on a hot day in May and on a cold night in December.
terms.art: A child in summer clothes and the same child in a sweater, with a thermometer reading 37 beside each.

terms.meaning: Albedo is the share of the sunlight falling on a surface that the surface reflects back. A pale surface has a high albedo. A dark surface has a low albedo.
terms.example: Fresh snow reflects most of the sunlight that falls on it. The dark sea reflects very little.
terms.art: Sun rays bouncing off a white snowfield and sinking into dark sea water.

terms.meaning: A model is a simple copy of a real thing, made to find out how the real thing might work. A model can be a drawing, a set of rules or a computer program.
terms.example: The Daisy Planet is a model. It has only daisies, a Sun and three rules.
terms.art: A hand-drawn grid of squares with dark and pale beans on it, beside a picture of the real Earth.

terms.meaning: A hypothesis is a possible explanation that can be tested against evidence.
terms.example: 'Living beings keep the Earth's temperature steady' is a hypothesis. Scientists test it against what the rocks and the air show.
terms.art: A notebook page with one sentence circled and a question mark beside it.

terms.meaning: The Gaia hypothesis says that the living beings of the Earth, together with the air, sea and rocks, form one system. It says this system keeps the Earth fit for life. Gaia is said 'guy-ah'.
terms.example: James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis put the Gaia hypothesis forward in the 1970s. Scientists still argue about it.
terms.art: The Earth drawn with looping arrows joining the forests, the sea, the clouds and the rocks.

terms.meaning: Phytoplankton are tiny living beings who float in the sea and in lakes. They make their food from carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight. Most are too small to see without a microscope.
terms.example: Phytoplankton make about half of all the oxygen that living beings make each year.
terms.art: A drop of sea water under a microscope, full of tiny green and golden cells.

explanations.definition: Ecologists study life at five levels. They are one organism, a population, a community, an ecosystem and the biosphere. Each level contains all the levels below it.
explanations.description: An ecologist is a scientist who studies how living beings live with each other and with their surroundings. One living being is an organism. All the organisms of one species in one place are a population. All the populations in that place, of every species, are a community. The community together with the water, air, soil and sunlight is an ecosystem. All the ecosystems of the Earth together are the biosphere. The levels are a way of looking, like zooming out with a camera. Nothing new is added to the world at each level. You only see more of what was already joined together.
examples: One lion-tailed macaque in a tree in Silent Valley, Kerala, is an organism. All the lion-tailed macaques of Silent Valley are a population.
The macaques, the trees, the hornbills, the frogs, the fungi and the soil microbes of Silent Valley are a community.
Add the streams, the rain, the soil and the mist, and Silent Valley is an ecosystem. Silent Valley is one small part of the biosphere.
explanations.art: Five circles, one inside the next, with a single monkey at the centre, then a troop of monkeys, then a forest full of different beings, then the forest with its stream and rain, then the whole Earth.

explanations.definition: Every level depends on the level above it for what it needs, and every level is made by the beings in the level below it.
explanations.description: Look upward first. One organism needs a population, because most animals and many plants need a mate to have young. A population needs a community, because its members need food, and many need other species to carry their pollen or seeds. A community needs an ecosystem, because every living being needs water, air and warmth. An ecosystem needs the biosphere, because its rain and its air come from far away. Now look downward. A population is only its organisms. A community is only its populations. The biosphere is only its ecosystems. So when the organisms change, every level above them changes too. Changes travel both ways, up and down.
examples: A single wild fig tree cannot make seeds alone. Each kind of fig needs their own kind of tiny fig wasp to carry the pollen.
A forest in the Western Ghats cannot make the monsoon. The wet wind comes from the Arabian Sea, thousands of kilometres of ocean away.
About 2,400 million years ago, tiny bacteria began to fill the air with oxygen. Organisms too small to see changed the whole biosphere.
explanations.art: A ladder with five rungs labelled organism, population, community, ecosystem and biosphere, with arrows going both up and down between the rungs.

explanations.concept: Emergent properties: what a whole has that its parts do not
explanations.definition: An emergent property is a feature that a whole has and that none of its parts has alone. It comes from the way the parts act on each other.
explanations.description: Each level of life has properties that the level below does not have. One crow cannot have a birth rate, but a population of crows can. One species cannot have a food web, but a community can. A community cannot have a water cycle, but an ecosystem can. These properties are real, and they can be measured. Yet you will not find them by looking at one part, however closely you look. That is why ecologists study each level in its own right. The reason is simple. The property comes from many parts acting on each other, so it needs many parts.
examples: Honeybees keep the part of the hive where their young grow at about 32 to 36 degrees Celsius. They shiver to warm it and fan their wings to cool it. One bee alone cannot hold any place at a steady temperature.
Pour rice slowly on a plate, and the heap always makes about the same slope. No single grain has a slope.
You can ride a cycle. No single cell of your body can ride one.
explanations.art: A cluster of honeybees on a honeycomb with a thermometer reading 35, beside one bee alone on a leaf.

explanations.concept: The biosphere is a very thin layer
explanations.definition: The biosphere is the part of the Earth where living beings are found. Compared with the size of the Earth, it is very thin.
explanations.description: The word biosphere was first used by the geologist Eduard Suess in 1875. In 1926 the Russian scientist Vladimir Vernadsky wrote a book called The Biosphere. He said that living beings are a force that shapes the planet, as strong as wind or water. Living beings have been found at the bottom of the deepest sea, about 11 kilometres down. A vulture has been recorded flying about 11 kilometres up. Microbes also live in rock several kilometres under the ground. So nearly all life is in a layer about 20 kilometres thick. The Earth is about 12,700 kilometres across. If the Earth were a ball 1 metre across, that layer would be less than 2 millimetres thick.
examples: A football is about 22 centimetres across. On an Earth that size, the biosphere would be thinner than half a millimetre.
Mount Everest is less than 9 kilometres high. Bar-headed geese cross the Himalayas flying more than 7 kilometres up.
explanations.art: The Earth cut in half like a fruit, with a hair-thin green line on the outside labelled 'all of life is here'.

explanations.concept: Energy passes through the biosphere, but matter stays and goes round
explanations.definition: The Earth takes in energy as sunlight and sends almost exactly the same amount back out to space. Almost no matter enters or leaves, so the same atoms are used again and again.
explanations.description: Sunlight reaches the Earth all the time. The Earth sends energy back out to space all the time, partly as reflected light and mostly as heat. If more came in than went out, the Earth would keep getting hotter. Matter is different. Apart from a little dust from space and a little gas that escapes, the Earth keeps the same atoms. So the biosphere has to recycle. The waste of one living being must be the food of another. Animals breathe out carbon dioxide, and plants take carbon dioxide in. Plants give out oxygen, and animals take oxygen in. From 1991 to 1993, eight people lived sealed inside a huge glass building in Arizona, in the United States, called Biosphere 2. It held a small rainforest, a small sea and a farm. Within sixteen months the oxygen in its air fell from about 21 parts in 100 to about 14. The soil had been made very rich in compost, and the microbes in the soil used up oxygen faster than the plants made it. Oxygen had to be pumped in. A working biosphere is much harder to build than anyone expected.
examples: A sealed glass jar with damp soil and a small plant can live for months on a windowsill. Light goes in and heat comes out, but no water or air is added.
The water you drank today has been drunk before, many times, by other animals and by plants.
explanations.art: The Earth with a yellow arrow of sunlight coming in, a red arrow of heat going out, and a closed green loop of arrows going round on its surface.

explanations.definition: The Earth's air is very different from the air of the planets next to it, and living beings are the reason. Nearly all the oxygen in the air was made by photosynthesis.
explanations.description: Photosynthesis is the way plants, seaweeds and some bacteria make food from carbon dioxide and water, using light. Oxygen is given out as they do it. The young Earth had almost no oxygen in its air. About 2,400 million years ago, bacteria called cyanobacteria had made so much oxygen that it began to stay in the air. Scientists call this the Great Oxidation Event. They know about it from rocks. Rocks older than that hold minerals that cannot last where there is oxygen. Today oxygen is 21 parts in every 100 of the air. Oxygen reacts easily. It rusts iron and it burns wood. So if living beings stopped making oxygen, the oxygen in the air would slowly be used up. No life has been found on Venus or Mars. Their air shows what a planet's air is like with no life at work. On both, 95 parts or more in every 100 are carbon dioxide.
examples: Phytoplankton in the sea do about half of all the photosynthesis on the Earth. Plants on land do the other half.
In 1986, Sallie Chisholm and her team found Prochlorococcus in the sea. They are the smallest and the most numerous of all the cells who photosynthesise.
The oxygen in the air built up over many millions of years. Each year, living beings use up almost as much oxygen as they make.
explanations.art: Three bars side by side for Venus, the Earth and Mars, each divided into coloured parts for carbon dioxide, nitrogen and oxygen.

explanations.concept: Living beings also move water, make soil and change the weather
explanations.definition: Living beings change the non-living parts of their ecosystems. Some of these changes reach far beyond the place where those beings live.
explanations.description: A tree draws water up from the soil and gives it out from her leaves as water vapour. A whole forest gives out so much that the vapour falls again as rain somewhere else. One study from the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay in 2018 used a computer model of the monsoon. It estimated that the forests of the Western Ghats supply 25 to 40 parts in every 100 of the monsoon rain that falls on Tamil Nadu. Soil is made by life too. Rock is broken up by roots, fungi and microbes, and mixed with dead leaves by earthworms and termites. Life even links ecosystems across an ocean. Wind carries dust from the Sahara desert in Africa to the Amazon rainforest in South America. The dust holds phosphorus, which plants need. Much of that dust comes from the dry bed of an old lake, and it is rich in the remains of tiny beings who lived in that lake.
examples: Stand under a big banyan on a hot afternoon. The air is cooler there, partly because the leaves are giving out water.
A satellite study in 2015 estimated that about 22,000 tonnes of phosphorus reach the Amazon in Sahara dust every year.
Coral animals built the islands of Lakshadweep. The land there was made by living beings.
explanations.art: A forested hill range with mist rising from the trees, the mist drifting east and falling as rain on dry fields.

explanations.definition: Feedback happens when the result of a change comes back and affects that change. Balancing feedback works against the change. Reinforcing feedback adds to it.
explanations.description: A system stays steady when it has balancing feedback. Your body is one example. When you get hot, you sweat, and the sweat cools you. When you get cold, you shiver, and the shivering warms you. In both cases the result works against the change. Reinforcing feedback does the opposite. A small change causes more of the same change, so things run away in one direction. Ice shows this. Ice is pale, so it reflects sunlight. If some ice melts, the dark ground or sea takes in more sunlight. That warms the place, and more ice melts. The Earth has many loops of both kinds, running at the same time. Whether the Earth stays steady depends on which loops are stronger.
examples: Balancing: more rats in a paddy field means more food for rat snakes. More snakes then eat more rats, so the rats become fewer again.
Reinforcing: a fire dries the leaves next to it. Dry leaves catch fire easily, so the fire spreads faster.
Balancing, but very slow: warm, wet weather wears rock away faster. Wearing rock takes carbon dioxide out of the air, and that cools the Earth over about a million years.
explanations.art: Two loops of arrows side by side, one drawn as a see-saw settling level, the other as a snowball growing as it rolls downhill.

explanations.description: In the 1960s, the scientist James Lovelock was asked to help look for life on Mars. He noticed how strange the Earth's air is compared with the air of Mars and Venus. In the 1970s he and the biologist Lynn Margulis put forward the Gaia hypothesis. It says that living beings, together with the air, the sea and the rocks, form one system that keeps the Earth fit for life. The name Gaia comes from an old Greek name for the Earth. Lovelock's neighbour, the writer William Golding, suggested it. Almost all scientists now agree with one part of the idea: life changes the planet a great deal. The part they argue about is whether life keeps the planet steady, and whether it is right to say the Earth acts as one whole.
examples: For: when life began, the Sun gave only about three quarters of the light it gives today. Yet the Earth has had liquid water for nearly all that time.
Against: between about 720 and 635 million years ago, the Earth froze almost completely, at least twice. The system did not hold steady then.

perspectives.explanation: Living beings and their surroundings together form one system with balancing feedback. That system has kept the temperature and the air of the Earth within the range that life can bear, for more than three thousand million years.

Living beings are shaped by natural selection. This means that those who leave more young pass on their features. Natural selection helps an organism or their family. It cannot make organisms work for the good of a whole planet. There is also only one Earth, so planets cannot have been selected against each other.

The hypothesis is said in many different ways. The weak forms are true but not new. The strong forms cannot be tested. Life makes reinforcing feedback as well as balancing feedback, so life can make conditions less steady too.

Life has often harmed life. When bacteria first filled the air with oxygen, that oxygen was probably a poison to most living beings of the time. Ward calls his idea the Medea hypothesis, after a mother in an old Greek story who harms her own children.
The Earth may have stayed fit for life partly through luck. We could only be here to ask the question on a planet where things went well. So a long steady record is not proof of a steadying system.

Scientists from four international research programmes agreed on this statement: the Earth behaves as a single, self-regulating system made of physical, chemical, biological and human parts. They did not say the system is sure to stay good for us.

explanations.art: A round table with six chairs, each with a name card, and a globe in the middle of the table.

explanations.concept: The Daisy Planet: what a model can show, and what it cannot
explanations.description: Critics said Gaia would need living beings to plan together for the good of the planet. In 1983, Andrew Watson and James Lovelock answered with a model called Daisyworld. Their planet has only dark daisies and pale daisies, under a Sun that slowly gets brighter. Dark daisies take in more sunlight, so they warm the ground. Pale daisies reflect more, so they cool it. Daisies only grow where the warmth suits them. Yet in the model, the planet's temperature stays almost level for a long time. The Daisy Planet Test in this unit is a simple paper version of that model. The model shows one thing clearly. Steadying can come from living beings who only grow where it suits them. No planning together is needed. But a model shows what could happen. It does not show what does happen on the real Earth. The real Earth has millions of species, and many of them push conditions away from steady.
examples: In the Daisy Planet Test, the bare planet warms from 8 to 47 degrees. The planet with daisies stays between 20 and 27 degrees for twelve rounds.
The model has a limit. When every square is full of pale daisies, the daisies can cool the planet no further, and the temperature starts to climb.

perspectives.explanation: The model proves that a planet can regulate its temperature without foresight or planning. The daisies only follow their own needs.
The model was built so that what is good for each daisy is also good for the planet. On the real Earth the two often differ. So the model shows that regulation is possible, not that it is likely.

explanations.art: A small grey planet covered in patches of dark daisies and pale daisies, under a large yellow Sun.

explanations.description: This is a question about what the word 'alive' means, as well as a question about the Earth. Living organisms take in energy, keep themselves steady, grow and have young. The Earth takes in energy and may keep itself steady. The Earth does not have young, and has no parents. People who think carefully about this do not agree, and the answer depends on which signs of life you count as the important ones.
examples: A honeybee colony keeps the hive's warmth steady, gathers food and founds new colonies. Many biologists call a colony a 'superorganism'.
A candle flame takes in fuel and keeps its shape, but almost nobody calls a flame alive.

perspectives.explanation: The Earth regulates itself in the way a living body does. So in his books he often wrote of the Earth as alive. He also said this was a way of speaking, to help people see the Earth as one system.

She did not like calling the Earth one organism. She pointed out that no organism eats its own waste, but the biosphere recycles everything. She saw Gaia as a huge set of ecosystems acting on each other.

Living beings come from parents and are shaped by natural selection. The Earth has no parents, has no young and does not compete with other planets. So the Earth is a home for life, and not a living being.

perspectives.who: The Atharva Veda and many peoples who live close to forests and rivers
perspectives.explanation: The Earth is a mother, and living beings are her children. Many communities across India treat a hill, a river or a grove as a living someone, and protect them for that reason.

explanations.art: The Earth with a faint outline of a heartbeat line across it, and a question mark.

explanations.definition: Humans are one species among millions, but today humans change every level of life, up to the whole biosphere.
explanations.description: Other beings have changed the whole Earth before. Cyanobacteria did it with oxygen. Humans are now doing it with carbon dioxide. Coal, oil and gas are the remains of ancient living beings, and burning them puts their carbon into the air. Before factories, the air held about 280 parts of carbon dioxide in every million. Now it holds more than 420. Carbon dioxide traps heat, so the Earth is warming. The change is fast. Forests, seas and rocks do take carbon dioxide out of the air, but far more slowly than people are adding it. People have also mended a harm that reached the whole biosphere. In the 1970s, scientists found that gases from fridges and spray cans were destroying the ozone in the upper air. Ozone shields living beings from harmful rays of the Sun. In 1987 the countries of the world agreed to stop making those gases, and the ozone is slowly recovering.
examples: James Lovelock built the instrument that first measured those fridge gases in air far out at sea. It showed that they had spread across the world.
When a forest in the Western Ghats is cut, one hornbill loses her nest tree. Farms far to the east may also lose some of their rain.
explanations.art: A line graph of carbon dioxide in the air rising steeply, drawn over a faint picture of chimneys on one side and a forest on the other.

agreed.text: Life can be studied at five levels: organism, population, community, ecosystem and biosphere. Each level has properties the level below does not have.
agreed.evidence: A birth rate can be measured only for a population. A food web can be drawn only for a community. A water cycle can be traced only through an ecosystem.

agreed.text: Nearly all the oxygen in the Earth's air was made by living beings through photosynthesis.
agreed.evidence: Rocks older than about 2,400 million years hold minerals that cannot last in air with oxygen. Younger rocks do not. Mars and Venus, with no known life, have almost no oxygen in their air.

agreed.text: Living beings change the air, water, soil and climate around them, sometimes across the whole Earth.
agreed.evidence: Measurements show forests returning rain to the air, microbes and roots turning rock into soil, and phytoplankton doing about half of the Earth's photosynthesis.

agreed.text: The Earth has both balancing and reinforcing feedback loops, and living beings take part in both kinds.
agreed.evidence: Melting ice speeds up warming, which is reinforcing. Warm weather wears rock faster and that removes carbon dioxide from the air, which is balancing. Both have been measured.

agreed.text: The Earth has had liquid water and living beings for more than 3,500 million years, though the young Sun gave only about three quarters of today's light.
agreed.evidence: The oldest signs of life in rocks are about 3,500 million years old or older. Rocks formed in water are found from every age since.

agreed.text: The Earth has not always been steady. It has been almost completely frozen, and it has been much hotter than today.
agreed.evidence: Rocks dropped by ice are found in places that were near the equator between about 720 and 635 million years ago.

challenging.claim: The Earth regulates itself for the good of life.
challenging.who: James Lovelock, in his early writing on Gaia in the 1970s
challenging.for: The air and the temperature have stayed within the range life can bear for a very long time, while the Sun grew brighter. Living beings are part of many balancing loops.
challenging.against: Natural selection cannot make living beings work for a planet's good. Life has also caused disasters, such as the first spread of oxygen. Lovelock later said that the regulation is not done on purpose.
challenging.context: This card is about the strongest form of the Gaia idea: that the Earth keeps itself fit for life on purpose.

challenging.claim: The Amazon rainforest makes 20 parts in every 100 of the oxygen we breathe.
challenging.for: The Amazon is huge, and the trees there do a great deal of photosynthesis.
challenging.against: The trees, animals and microbes of the forest use up almost all the oxygen that the forest makes. So the forest adds almost nothing to the oxygen in the air. The Amazon matters greatly for rain, for carbon and for the millions of beings who live there.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular saying: that the Amazon rainforest is 'the lungs of the Earth'.

challenging.claim: Living beings fit themselves to their surroundings, and the surroundings stay as they are.
challenging.for: A camel is suited to the desert and a fish to the water. Living beings clearly are shaped by where they live.
challenging.against: Living beings also shape where they live. Bacteria and plants made the oxygen in the air. Earthworms and microbes make soil. Forests make some of their own rain. The fitting goes both ways.
challenging.context: This card is about the common idea that the surroundings of living beings are fixed, and only the living beings change.

challenging.claim: Life makes the Earth worse for life as often as it makes it better.
challenging.who: Peter Ward, in his book The Medea Hypothesis, 2009
challenging.for: Oxygen from the first photosynthesising bacteria poisoned most life of the time. Several of the great die-offs in Earth's history may have been set off by living beings.
challenging.against: After each disaster, life spread again in new forms. Over the whole record, the Earth has stayed fit for life. Most scientists think Ward shows that Gaia is too simple, not that the opposite is true.
challenging.context: This card is about the Medea hypothesis, which is the opposite of the Gaia hypothesis.

challenging.claim: The Daisy Planet model proves that Gaia is real.
challenging.for: The model does regulate its temperature, with no planning by the daisies.
challenging.against: A model shows what could happen under its own rules. The rules were chosen so that each daisy's needs match the planet's needs. Whether the real Earth works that way has to be tested on the real Earth.
challenging.context: This card is about what a model, such as the Daisy Planet, can and cannot prove.

big_questions.q: The oxygen you breathe was made by other beings, and the carbon dioxide you breathe out feeds plants. So where does your body end?
big_questions.hint: Follow one breath in and one breath out. Which living beings touched that air before you and after you?

big_questions.q: A population has a birth rate, but no single crow has one. Is a population a real thing, or only a word for many crows?
big_questions.hint: Think of the rice heap. Is the slope real? Where is it?

big_questions.q: The Earth takes in energy and may keep itself steady, but has no young. Would you call the Earth alive? What would change your mind?
big_questions.hint: List the signs of life you know. Which ones does the Earth show? Does a bee colony show them?

big_questions.q: In the Daisy Planet Test, the planet stayed steady though the daisies only grew where it suited them. Can a good result for all come from each one following their own needs?
big_questions.hint: Then think of the round when every square was full. What happened next?

big_questions.q: We could only be here on a planet that stayed fit for life. So is our steady Earth good evidence for a steadying system, or just luck?
big_questions.hint: Imagine a hundred planets. On which ones would there be anyone to ask this question?

big_questions.q: Cyanobacteria changed the whole Earth with oxygen and never knew. Humans are changing it with carbon dioxide and do know. What difference does knowing make?
big_questions.hint: Think about the fridge gases and the ozone layer. What did people do once they knew?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that living beings make the air of a planet? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: Sixty years ago, most scientists treated a planet's air as the work of volcanoes, rocks and sunlight. They knew that plants give out oxygen. But few thought that living beings decide what the whole air is made of. In the 1960s, the American space agency NASA was planning to look for life on Mars. It asked the scientist James Lovelock to help. Lovelock and the philosopher Dian Hitchcock said nobody needed to land a machine to dig in the soil. They said to look at the air of Mars through a telescope. On a planet with no life, the gases in the air will have reacted with each other until nothing more can happen. The Earth's air is not like that. It holds oxygen and methane together, and those two gases destroy each other. Living beings must be making both all the time. The air of Mars turned out to be almost all carbon dioxide, with nothing still reacting. Hitchcock and Lovelock published the idea in 1967. So on the Earth, living beings decide what the air is made of. Scientists now use the same test to look for life on planets around other stars.
how_we_found_out.who: James Lovelock and Dian Hitchcock, who worked out how to find life from a planet's air. Lynn Margulis, who showed which microbes make which gases.
how_we_found_out.when: 1965 (Lovelock's first paper on the idea), 1967 (Hitchcock and Lovelock's paper) and 1974 (Lovelock and Margulis's paper on the Gaia hypothesis)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That volcanoes, rocks and sunlight decide what a planet's air is made of, and living beings only fit themselves to it. The Earth's air holds gases that destroy each other, such as oxygen and methane. They can only stay there because living beings keep making them.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman and a man in 1960s clothes at a desk with a chart of three planets' air, and a telescope by the window.

story.title: The Line Nobody Drew
story.note: A made-up story. Koodu, the farm near Kotagiri and all the people in it are imagined. The science is real, and it comes from a real event. From 1991 to 1993, eight people lived sealed inside a glass building called Biosphere 2 in Arizona, in the United States. The oxygen in their air fell from about 21 parts in 100 to about 14. The cause was the microbes in the rich soil, who were using up oxygen faster than the plants could make it. Oxygen had to be pumped in. A compost heap really does warm up and steam on a cold morning, because the microbes in the heap give out heat as they respire.
text: Every evening at six, Kayal walked up the tea slope to the glass house and pressed her palm flat against the wall. On the other side, her mother pressed back. The glass was cold, and as thick as a thumb.

The glass house was called Koodu, which means nest. Three women had been sealed inside it for fifty-two days. Nothing went in and nothing came out, except sunlight, and voices on the telephone. Their water went round and round. Their air went round and round. They grew their food in long beds of black soil, and the plants in the beds made the oxygen the women breathed. If three people could live a hundred days like that on a hillside near Kotagiri, people might one day live like that much further away.
Kayal was ten. She lived for these months with Shanthi Athai, her aunt, who ran the compost yard at the bottom of the farm.
"You look tired, Amma," Kayal said into the telephone.
"I climbed the ladder to the bean vines," her mother said, and laughed. "Eleven steps. I had to sit down at the top." She laughed again, but Kayal saw her hand go to her chest.

On the wall by the door was a board with numbers, for anyone outside to read. Kayal read them every day, as other children read cricket scores. Water: steady. Carbon dioxide: steady, because a machine inside caught the extra and held it. Oxygen: 17.9.
On the first day the oxygen had been 21, the same as on the hillside. Kayal had the whole column in her notebook. It went down like stairs.
Prakash sir, the engineer, was on his knees by the wall again with a brush and a tin of soapy water. He painted the soap along every joint in the glass and watched for bubbles.
"Still looking for the leak, sir?"

"There must be a leak." He sat back on his heels. "The plants are healthy. The lamps are fine. I counted the leaves myself. Those plants make enough oxygen for three people, with some to spare. So where is the oxygen going?"

Kayal thought about it on the way down the slope. If there was a hole, air would come in from the hillside. The air on the hillside was 21. A hole would push the number up, and the number was going down. She did not say so. He was a kind man, and he had not slept much.

The next morning was the coldest of the year. There was frost on the tea, white and thin, like sugar on a plate. Athai woke her before the sun was up. "The big heap must be turned today. Come and hold the lamp."
The heap stood taller than Kayal, a long dark hill of leaves, cow dung and kitchen peelings from the whole farm. Athai drove the fork in and pulled.

Steam poured out. It rose in the lamplight, thick as the steam off a pot of rice. Kayal pulled off her glove and held her hand over the hole. The air coming out was warm. The inside of the heap was hot, on a morning of frost.
"Who lit a fire in there?"

"Nobody lit anything." Athai turned another forkful. "They are eating. More of them in one handful than there are people in India. Eating all night, and breathing all night. That is where the heat comes from."
"Breathing?"

"Why do you think I turn the heap? If I leave them packed tight, they use up the air inside and the heap goes sour. They need air as much as you do." She pushed the fork in again. "More than you do. There are more of them."
Kayal stood very still, with the lamp in her hand and the steam going past her face.

She was remembering a morning two months ago. A line of people with sacks on their shoulders, walking up the slope to Koodu before the door was sealed. Sixty sacks. Athai had stood at the gate, counting them out, proud. Her best compost, two years old, black as coffee powder, for the vegetable beds.
"Athai. How many people are breathing inside Koodu?"
"Three. You know that."
"And the hens?"
"Four hens."
"And who else?"
Athai stopped with the fork in the air. She looked at the heap. Then she looked up the hill at the glass, which was just turning pink.

Prakash sir did not laugh. He listened to all of it with his tea going cold. Then he fetched a big glass jar with a tight lid, and a small meter on a wire. He asked for a spadeful of soil from the same sacks. There were two left over in the shed. He put the soil in the jar with the meter, screwed the lid down and wrote the time on it.
"Twenty-one," he said. "Now we wait."
By evening the meter in the jar said nineteen. By the next morning it said sixteen. There was no plant in the jar and no person. There was only soil, sitting quietly in the dark.

He took the jar up to the glass and held it against the wall for the three women to see. Kayal's mother read the number. She looked at the long black beds behind her, and then she put both hands over her mouth.

That afternoon she unrolled the big plan of Koodu on the floor inside, where Kayal could see it through the glass. It was a drawing of everything that breathed in and everything that breathed out, with an arrow for each. There was an arrow for each woman. There was one for the hens, and one for the beans, the tomatoes and the greens.
"We counted everybody," her mother said into the telephone. Her voice was thin. "We were so careful."
"You counted everybody you could see," said Kayal.
Her mother took a pencil. Under the beds on the plan she drew one more arrow. It was thicker than all the others.

They did not break the seal. A cylinder of oxygen went in through the small hatch that week, and half the compost came out in the same sacks. Athai counted them back at the gate, and said nothing, and patted each one as it passed.
The numbers on the board began to climb, slowly, like someone going up a ladder and stopping to rest.
On the morning it reached 20, Kayal went down to the yard before school. She pulled off her glove and held her hand over the big heap. It was warm.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the three women, the hens and the plants were not the only beings breathing the air of the sealed house. The soil held countless microbes, and they were using oxygen too. A living place is a whole system, and the beings nobody sees are part of the system. Kayal works it out from the steaming compost heap. Let your child reach this before you say it.
ask: Why did Kayal think a hole in the glass could not explain the falling oxygen number?
What did the steam from the compost heap show?
The plan had an arrow for everyone who breathes. Who was left out, and why?
Who breathes the air in your home, besides the people?
The Earth is sealed too. Nothing much comes in except sunlight. What do you think keeps the Earth's oxygen from running down?

roots.context: We have learned that life is arranged in levels, and that living beings have changed the air and the warmth of the whole Earth. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Daisy Planet Test, the planet's warmth decided which daisies grew. The daisies then changed the planet's warmth. The oxygen in the air was made by living beings, and that oxygen decides who can live here now. So living beings and the place they live in keep making each other.
deep_truth.habit: We say that living beings 'adapt to their environment'. That makes the environment sound like a fixed stage that was there first. The air, the soil and some of the rain were made by living beings, so the stage is partly made by the actors.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Daisy Planet Test, the bare planet warmed from 8 to 47 degrees, but the planet with daisies stayed between 20 and 27 degrees for twelve rounds. On the real Earth, rocks older than about 2,400 million years show that the air once had almost no oxygen. Bacteria and plants made it.

three.who_am_i: You are one organism. You are also part of a population, a community, an ecosystem and the biosphere, all at the same moment. Each breath you take was prepared by other living beings.
three.what_is_life: Life does not only live on the Earth. Life has changed the Earth's air, soil and rain, and those changes have changed life in turn.
three.what_is_this_world: The world around you is partly made by the living. The air in this room would be a different air if nothing had ever lived on the Earth.

roots.thread: A crow looks like one separate thing. Zoom out, and the crow is part of a population, then a community, then an ecosystem, then the biosphere. At no step do you reach a place where the crow stops and the rest begins. The crow's breath is the forest's air, and the forest's air is the whole Earth's air. Consciousness is in everything, and so it is in the Earth as a whole. Many scientists who accept everything else in this unit say the Earth is a system and not a mind.

teachings.teaching: The Earth is my mother, and I am her son.
teachings.link: This hymn was sung long before anyone could measure the air. The science agrees with the plain part of it. Every atom of your body, and every breath, came to you from the Earth and the living beings on the Earth.
verse: यत्ते मध्यं पृथिवि यच्च नभ्यं यास्त ऊर्जस्तन्वः संबभूवुः ।
तासु नो धेह्यभि नः पवस्व माता भूमिः पुत्रो अहं पृथिव्याः पर्जन्यः पिता स उ नः पिपर्तु

teachings.teaching: Always think of the universe as one living being, with one substance and one soul. See how all things work together to cause all that happens.
teachings.link: Marcus Aurelius was a Roman emperor who wrote this about 1,850 years ago. The Gaia hypothesis asks a smaller question about just one planet: do the living and the non-living parts of the Earth work together as one system?

καὶ πῶς ὁρμῇ μιᾷ πάντα πράσσει καὶ πῶς πάντα πάντων τῶν γινομένων συναίτια

teachings.teaching: If the world cannot go on without water, then water cannot go on without rain.
teachings.link: Thiruvalluvar saw that life depends on something far above any one field or village. Today we can add a step. Part of the rain depends on forests, so the rain also depends on life.

science.text: Nearly all the oxygen in the Earth's air was made by living beings.
The Earth behaves as one system in which living beings, air, sea and rock all affect each other.
Whether that system keeps the Earth fit for life, as the Gaia hypothesis says, is still argued about.

other_view.who: Richard Dawkins and many other biologists
other_view.view: The Earth is not a living being and has no aims. Each organism lives for themself and their family. If the planet has stayed fit for life, that is partly the result of many separate struggles and partly good luck. Calling the Earth one whole hides how much living beings compete.

practice.title: One breath, followed all the way
practice.say: Sit near a window with your eyes closed. Breathe in slowly through your nose. This oxygen was made by a leaf, or by a tiny green cell in the sea. Hold the breath for a moment. Now breathe out slowly. This carbon dioxide will drift out of the window. One day a leaf will take it in and build with it. Let's do five slow breaths like this. Then open your eyes and look at the nearest plant.
practice.kid: Sit by a window and close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. A leaf or a sea cell made this oxygen. Breathe out slowly. A leaf will use this carbon dioxide one day. Take five slow breaths. Then open your eyes and look at a plant.

ask: Your breath was made by other beings, and your breath feeds other beings. Is the air outside you a part of you?
The daisies changed the planet, and the planet changed the daisies. Which one was in charge?
The Earth has no parents and no young. Is that enough to say the Earth is not alive?

games.title: Which Level?
games.context: This is a card game about the five levels of life. Each card names one living being or a group of them. You say which level that is: organism, population, community, ecosystem or biosphere.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: One banyan tree in a garden in Adyar, Chennai
items.b: Organism. This is one living being.

items.f: The gecko on your kitchen wall tonight
items.b: Organism. This is one living being.

items.f: One bacterium in a spoon of curd
items.b: Organism. A single cell can be a whole living being.

items.f: You
items.b: Organism. You are one living being. Your body is also home to many others.

items.f: One olive ridley turtle laying her eggs on a beach in Odisha
items.b: Organism. She is one living being.

items.f: All the Asiatic lions of the Gir forest in Gujarat
items.b: Population. They are all the members of one species in one place.

items.f: All the house sparrows of Mysuru
items.b: Population. They are one species in one place.

items.f: All the neem trees of one village
items.b: Population. They are one species in one place.

items.f: All the Nilgiri tahr on the hills of Eravikulam in Kerala
items.b: Population. A Nilgiri tahr is a wild mountain goat. These are one species in one place.

items.f: All the people of Kochi
items.b: Population. Humans are one species of animal, and these are the humans of one place.

items.f: The trees, crabs, fish, birds and microbes of the Pichavaram mangrove, without the water or the mud
items.b: Community. These are many species in one place, with the non-living things left out.

items.f: All the tea bushes, shade trees, insects, birds and soil fungi of one tea garden in Assam
items.b: Community. These are all the species of one place.

items.f: The hundreds of kinds of bacteria who live in your gut
items.b: Community. They are many species living together in one place.

items.f: The corals, fish, seaweeds and crabs of one reef in Lakshadweep
items.b: Community. These are many species in one place.

items.f: Every plant, animal and fungus of a shola forest in the Nilgiris, without the soil or the streams
items.b: Community. The living beings are counted, and the non-living things are not.

items.f: Chilika lake in Odisha: the water, mud and salt, with the fish, dolphins, birds and plants
items.b: Ecosystem. This is a community together with the non-living things around them.

items.f: A rotting log, with the fungi and beetles, the damp wood and the air in the cracks
items.b: Ecosystem. Even a small place is an ecosystem when you count the living and the non-living together.

items.f: The Thar desert: the sand, the heat and the wind, with all the plants and animals
items.b: Ecosystem. This is a community with their non-living surroundings.

items.f: A paddy field in Thanjavur: the water, mud and sunlight, with the rice, frogs, snails and microbes
items.b: Ecosystem. The living and the non-living are counted together.

items.f: A sealed glass jar holding soil, water, air and a small plant
items.b: Ecosystem. It is a very small one, with living and non-living parts.

items.f: Every place on the Earth where anything lives, taken together
items.b: Biosphere. This is the highest level.

items.f: All the oceans, forests, deserts, fields and cities, with everyone who lives in them
items.b: Biosphere. All the ecosystems together make the biosphere.

items.f: The thin layer of the Earth, about 20 kilometres thick, that holds nearly all life
items.b: Biosphere. The layer reaches from the deepest sea to the highest-flying birds.

items.f: All the ecosystems of the Earth, joined by one air and one ocean
items.b: Biosphere. The air and the sea join every ecosystem to the others.

ask.q: How do you tell a community from an ecosystem?
good: A community is only the living beings.
An ecosystem also counts the water, air, soil and sunlight.

flow.parent: The hardest cards are the community and ecosystem ones. The clue is whether water, mud, soil or air is on the card.

options: The water, mud, air and sunlight
check.why: An ecosystem is a community together with the non-living things around them. Adding other ponds would be a step towards the biosphere, not towards an ecosystem.

games.title: Push Back or Push On?
games.context: This is a card game about feedback. Each card describes a loop. You say whether the loop pushes back against the change, which is balancing feedback, or pushes the change on, which is reinforcing feedback.

printables.title: 16 two-sided cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: You run and get hot. You sweat. The sweat dries and cools your skin.
items.b: Push back: balancing. The sweat works against the heat.

items.f: Sea ice melts. Dark water is left. Dark water takes in more sunlight than ice did. The sea warms.
items.b: Push on: reinforcing. Warming melts ice, and less ice means more warming.

items.f: A room gets warm. The air-conditioner switches on. When the room is cool, it switches off.
items.b: Push back: balancing. The cooling works against the warming.

items.f: A fire dries the leaves next to it. Dry leaves catch fire easily.
items.b: Push on: reinforcing. The more fire there is, the faster it spreads.

items.f: There are more rats in a paddy field. So the rat snakes there find more food and raise more young.
items.b: Push back: balancing. More snakes eat more rats, so the rats become fewer again.

items.f: The Daisy Planet goes above 25 degrees. Pale daisies grow. Pale daisies reflect sunlight.
items.b: Push back: balancing. The pale daisies cool the planet.

items.f: A microphone is held near its own loudspeaker. The loudspeaker's sound goes into the microphone and comes out louder.
items.b: Push on: reinforcing. The sound grows into a loud squeal.

items.f: You eat a sweet. The sugar in your blood rises. Your body sends out insulin, and your cells take in the sugar.
items.b: Push back: balancing. Insulin brings the sugar in the blood down again.

items.f: One person in a hall starts to clap. People who hear clapping join in. The clapping gets louder.
items.b: Push on: reinforcing. More clapping brings still more clapping.

items.f: You step into a cold wind. You start to shiver. Shivering muscles give out heat.
items.b: Push back: balancing. The shivering works against the cold.

items.f: The Earth warms. In warm, wet weather, rock wears away faster. Wearing rock takes carbon dioxide out of the air.
items.b: Push back: balancing. Less carbon dioxide means less heat is trapped. This loop takes about a million years.

items.f: The Arctic warms. Frozen ground thaws. The thawed ground gives out gases that trap heat.
items.b: Push on: reinforcing. Warming brings more warming.

items.f: A beehive gets too warm. Worker bees fan their wings at the entrance.
items.b: Push back: balancing. The moving air cools the hive.

items.f: The Daisy Planet goes above 40 degrees. All the pale daisies die. The bare ground reflects less sunlight.
items.b: Push on: reinforcing. Losing the daisies makes the planet hotter still.

items.f: Rain washes soil off a bare hillside. With less soil, fewer plants can take root. Roots are what hold soil.
items.b: Push on: reinforcing. Less soil means fewer plants, and fewer plants means still less soil.

items.f: Tiny algae multiply in a tank. So the tiny animals who eat algae multiply too.
items.b: Push back: balancing. More eaters bring the algae down again.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say 'push back' if the loop works against the change, or 'push on' if the loop adds to it.
Turn the card over to check. Score 1 point if you were right.
Score 1 more point if you can say what would happen next, if the loop went on.
Stop when the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: sort the cards into a 'push back' pile and a 'push on' pile. Then turn them over and count how many are right.

flow.say: Some loops push back against a change, so things stay steady. Some loops push the change on, so it grows. Each card is one loop. We say which kind it is.
flow.kid: Cut out the 16 cards. Some loops push back against a change. Some loops push the change on. Shuffle the cards and make a pile.
flow.parent: Scientists call 'push back' loops balancing or negative feedback, and 'push on' loops reinforcing or positive feedback.
flow.context: This is the first step of Push Back or Push On? Here you cut out the cards and learn the two kinds of feedback loop.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card and say 'push back' or 'push on'. 2. Turn the card over to check, and score 1 point if right. 3. For 1 more point, say what would happen next if the loop went on. 4. Go on until the pile is finished.
flow.say: Read the card. Something changes. Does the last thing on the card work against that change, or add to it?
flow.kid: Read the top card. Say 'push back' or 'push on'. Turn the card to check. Right is 1 point. Say what happens next, for 1 more.

ask.q: How can you tell which kind of loop a card shows?
good: Follow the change all the way round. If it comes back smaller, the loop pushes back.
If it comes back bigger, the loop pushes on.

flow.context: This is the main step of Push Back or Push On? You read each card and say whether the loop works against the change or adds to it.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Put the 8 'push back' cards in one row and the 8 'push on' cards in another. 3. Ask which row holds the things that stay steady, and which holds the things that run away.
flow.say: Look at the two rows. Which row is full of things that stay steady? Which row is full of things that run away?
flow.kid: Count your points. Make a 'push back' row and a 'push on' row. Which row stays steady? Which row runs away?

check.q: Snow melts and leaves dark ground. The dark ground warms and melts more snow. What kind of feedback is this?
options: Reinforcing, because melting leads to more melting
Balancing, because the ground is dark
check.why: The result of the melting, which is dark ground, causes more melting. The change adds to itself, so the loop is reinforcing. Whether a thing is cold or dark does not decide the kind of loop.

flow.context: This is the last step of Push Back or Push On? Here you count the points and compare the balancing loops with the reinforcing loops.

experiments.title: The Daisy Planet Test: can daisies change the temperature of a whole planet?
experiments.context: In this experiment you run a paper planet with beans for daisies. Dark daisies warm the planet and pale daisies cool it. The Sun gets hotter every round. You find out if daisies can stop a planet from getting too hot while the Sun gets hotter.
experiments.question: The Sun gets 3 degrees hotter every round for 14 rounds. Does a planet with dark and pale daisies heat up as fast as a bare planet?
experiments.predict: Guess first. The bare planet will warm from 8 degrees to 47 degrees. Will the planet with daisies warm just as fast, warm more slowly, or stay about the same? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Both planets get the same Sun number in every round. The only difference is that one planet has daisies. Follow the three rules exactly in every round, and do not skip a round.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, A4 size or bigger
a ruler and a pencil
dark beans for dark daisies, such as rajma or black chana (dark buttons also work)
pale beans for pale daisies, such as kabuli chana or groundnuts (small balls of white paper also work)
a notebook, and squared paper for the graph
pencils of two colours

schedule.what: Draw the planet and the table. Learn the three rules. Guess. Play 14 rounds. Draw the two lines and explain them.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all 14 rounds. Draw a graph with two lines, one for the bare planet and one for the daisy planet. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: The bare planet: temperature in each round
example_chart.note: This is the planet with no daisies. Its temperature is the Sun number. Your second line, for the daisy planet, goes on the same graph.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a grid of 20 empty squares, four rows of five, and two small bowls beside it, one of dark beans and one of pale beans.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 20 squares for the planet's ground. Keep dark and pale beans ready.

setup.art: The same grid with six dark beans on six squares, and a notebook table beside it with the first three rows filled in.
setup.caption: 2. Each round, work out the temperature. Then add or take away daisies by the rules.

setup.art: A hand-drawn graph with two lines, one climbing steeply and one that rises and then runs almost level.
setup.caption: 3. After 14 rounds, draw one line for the bare planet and one for the daisy planet.

flow.do: 1. On the sheet, draw a grid of 20 squares, in 4 rows of 5. Make each square about 4 centimetres wide. 2. Write DAISY PLANET above the grid. 3. Count out 20 dark beans and 20 pale beans. 4. In the notebook, draw a table with 5 columns and 15 rows. 5. Head the columns: Round, Sun number, Dark daisies, Pale daisies, Temperature. 6. In the Sun number column write 8, 11, 14 and so on, adding 3 each time, up to 47.
flow.say: This grid is the ground of a small planet. Each square has room for one daisy. A dark bean is a dark daisy, and a pale bean is a pale daisy. The Sun number says how warm the planet would be with bare ground.
flow.kid: Draw 20 squares, 4 rows of 5. Count 20 dark beans and 20 pale beans. Draw a table with 5 columns. Write the Sun numbers: 8, 11, 14, up to 47.
flow.parent: The 14 Sun numbers are 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26, 29, 32, 35, 38, 41, 44 and 47. The bare planet's temperature is always the Sun number, so that column is the first line of the graph.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Daisy Planet Test. Here you draw the planet's ground and the results table.

flow.do: 1. Write the three rules on a slip of paper and keep it beside the planet. 2. Rule 1: the temperature is the Sun number, plus 1 for each dark daisy, minus 1 for each pale daisy. 3. Rule 2: if the temperature is below 20, take off 3 pale daisies and add 3 dark daisies. 4. Rule 3: if the temperature is above 25, take off 3 dark daisies and add 3 pale daisies. 5. If the temperature is from 20 to 25, change nothing. 6. Do round 1 together. The Sun number is 8 and there are no daisies, so the temperature is 8. That is below 20, so put 3 dark daisies on the planet.
flow.say: Dark daisies soak up sunlight, so they warm the ground a little. Pale daisies reflect sunlight, so they cool the ground a little. Daisies grow best between 20 and 25 degrees. When the planet is cold, the dark daisies do well, because they are warmer than the ground around them. When the planet is hot, the pale daisies do well, because they stay cooler.
flow.kid: Write the three rules on a slip. Do round 1 with a grown-up. The Sun number is 8. There are no daisies yet. So the temperature is 8. That is below 20. Put on 3 dark daisies.
flow.parent: A new daisy needs an empty square. If fewer than 3 daisies of a colour are on the planet, take off the ones that are there. If fewer than 3 squares are empty, fill the ones that are. The daisies you add or take away in one round count from the next round.
flow.context: This step of the Daisy Planet Test teaches the three rules. You play round 1 together to see how they work.

flow.do: 1. Point to the Sun number column. 2. Say that the bare planet will warm from 8 degrees to 47 degrees. 3. Ask what the planet with daisies will do, and why. 4. Write the guess and the reason in the notebook.
flow.say: The bare planet goes from 8 degrees to 47 degrees. What do you think the daisy planet will do? Will it warm just as fast, more slowly, or stay about the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The bare planet warms from 8 to 47 degrees. What will the daisy planet do? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: It will warm just as fast, because the Sun is the same for both. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
It will warm more slowly, because pale daisies cool it.
It will be hotter, because dark daisies warm it. (A fair guess. The test will show.)

flow.parent: Do not say which guess is right. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This step of the Daisy Planet Test is for guessing. You guess how the planet with daisies will warm, compared with a bare planet, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds 2 to 14, one at a time. 2. In each round, count the dark daisies and the pale daisies and write both numbers. 3. Work out the temperature with rule 1 and write it down. 4. Then use rule 2 or rule 3 to change the daisies for the next round. 5. Let your child do the sums and move the beans.
flow.say: Count the dark daisies and the pale daisies. Now work out the temperature. Is it below 20, above 25, or in between?
flow.kid: Play rounds 2 to 14. Each round, count the dark and pale daisies. Work out the temperature. Write it down. Then change the daisies by the rules.

ask.q: In round 5 the temperature goes above 25 for the first time. What happens to the daisies then?
good: Three dark daisies come off and three pale daisies go on.
The pale daisies start to grow, because the planet is too warm for the dark ones.

flow.parent: The rules always give the same answers, so you can check each round. The daisy planet's temperatures for rounds 1 to 14 are 8, 14, 20, 23, 26, 23, 26, 23, 26, 26, 26, 26, 26 and 27. The dark daisies go 0, 3, 6, 6, 6, 3, 3 and then 0. The pale daisies go 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 3, 6, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 and 20. If your numbers differ, look for a slip in that round and carry on from there.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Daisy Planet Test. In each of 13 more rounds you work out the planet's temperature and change the daisies by the rules.

flow.do: 1. On squared paper, draw a line across the bottom for rounds 1 to 14. 2. Draw a line up the side for temperature, from 0 to 50 degrees. 3. In one colour, mark the bare planet's temperature for each round, and join the marks. 4. In the other colour, mark the daisy planet's temperature for each round, and join the marks. 5. Shade the band from 20 to 25 degrees lightly with pencil.
flow.say: Let's draw both planets on one graph. One line is the bare planet, and the other is the planet with daisies. Shade the band where daisies grow best.
flow.kid: Draw rounds along the bottom. Draw temperature up the side. Mark the bare planet in one colour. Mark the daisy planet in the other colour. Join the marks. Shade from 20 to 25. No pencil to hand? Lay a bean at the right height for each round instead.
flow.parent: The bare planet's line is straight and steep. The daisy planet's line climbs quickly at first and then runs almost level, just above the shaded band.
flow.context: This step of the Daisy Planet Test is for drawing. You draw the temperatures of the bare planet and the daisy planet as two lines on one graph.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 2. Count the rounds in which each planet was between 20 and 27 degrees. 3. Ask what the model leaves out. 4. Only then read the explanation card called 'The Daisy Planet: what a model can show, and what it cannot'.
flow.say: What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen? Then tell me one thing about a real planet that our paper planet leaves out.
flow.kid: Look at your table and graph. Tell your grown-up the story of the Daisy Planet.

ask.q: Why did the daisy planet stay near 26 degrees while the Sun got hotter?
good: Each time it got too warm, more pale daisies grew, and they cooled it.
The daisies changed the temperature, and the temperature changed the daisies, so it kept coming back.

ask.q: Did any daisy have to plan to cool the planet?
good: No. Each kind of daisy grew when the warmth suited them.
No. The cooling came from many daisies together.

ask.q: What does the paper planet leave out?
good: Rain, clouds, seas, animals and many other kinds of plants.
Real daisies do not grow exactly 3 at a time.
A planet has warm and cold places, not one temperature.

flow.parent: The bare planet is between 20 and 27 degrees in 3 rounds: rounds 5, 6 and 7. The daisy planet is in that range in 12 rounds: rounds 3 to 14. Scientists call this kind of loop balancing feedback.

check.q: In the Daisy Planet Test, why did the planet with daisies stay near 26 degrees?
options: Pale daisies grew when it got too warm
The daisies agreed to cool the planet
check.why: Whenever the planet went above 25 degrees, pale daisies replaced dark ones, and pale daisies reflect sunlight. No agreement was needed. Choosing 'the Sun stopped' misses that the Sun number rose by 3 every round.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Daisy Planet Test. Here you say what you thought, what you saw and why, and what the paper model leaves out.

experiments.title: Dark Cloth, Pale Cloth: does a dark thing really get warmer in sunlight?
experiments.context: In the Daisy Planet Test, one rule said that dark daisies warm the ground and pale daisies cool it. In this experiment you test that rule with two tumblers of water in sunlight. One is wrapped in dark cloth and one in pale cloth.
experiments.question: Two tumblers of water stand in the same sunlight for 30 minutes. One is wrapped in black cloth and one in white cloth. Which water ends up warmer, or are they the same?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After 30 minutes in the sun, which tumbler of water will be warmer: the one in black cloth, the one in white cloth, or neither? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Use two tumblers of the same size and material. Put the same amount of water from the same tap in each. Wrap both in one layer of the same kind of cloth. Stand them side by side in the same sunlight for the same time. Change only the colour of the cloth.
results_table: How the water feels at the start
How the water feels after 30 minutes
Temperature after 30 minutes, if you have a thermometer

materials.item: tumblers of the same size, glass or steel
a piece of black or dark blue cotton cloth, big enough to wrap one tumbler (an old T-shirt works)
a piece of white cotton cloth of the same kind and size
rubber bands or string
tap water
a sunny windowsill, balcony or doorstep
a thermometer, if you have one

experiments.safety: Do this where direct sunlight falls, but never look at the Sun. Put glass tumblers where they cannot be knocked over.

schedule.what: Wrap two tumblers, fill them and stand them in the sun. Guess. Wait 30 minutes and compare the water.

experiments.record: Write which one felt warmer, and the two temperatures if you measured them. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: water temperature after 30 minutes in the sun
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Two identical glass tumblers, one wrapped in black cloth and one in white cloth, each held with a rubber band, being filled from a jug.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap one tumbler in black cloth and one in white. Pour the same amount of water into each.

setup.art: The two wrapped tumblers side by side on a sunny windowsill, with a clock beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Stand both in the same sunlight for 30 minutes.

setup.art: A child dipping one finger of each hand into the two tumblers at the same time.
setup.caption: 3. Dip a finger of each hand into the two tumblers. Which water is warmer?

flow.do: 1. Wrap one tumbler in black cloth and the other in white cloth. Cover the sides fully, in one layer. 2. Hold each cloth on with a rubber band. 3. Pour 100 millilitres of tap water into each tumbler. That is about half a small tumbler. 4. Ask your child to dip a finger of each hand into the two tumblers. They should feel the same.
flow.say: Both tumblers have the same water from the same tap. Dip a finger in each. Do they feel the same now?
flow.kid: Wrap one tumbler in black cloth. Wrap the other in white cloth. Pour the same water into each. Dip a finger in each.
flow.parent: If you have a thermometer, measure both now. They should agree to within one degree.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dark Cloth, Pale Cloth. Here you wrap two tumblers, one in black cloth and one in white, and fill them with the same water.

flow.do: 1. Stand both tumblers side by side in direct sunlight. 2. Check that no shadow falls on either one. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write them down. 4. Note the time.
flow.say: Both will stand in the same sun for 30 minutes. Which water will be warmer at the end? Or will they be the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stand both tumblers in the sun. Which water will be warmer after 30 minutes? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The black one, because dark clothes feel hotter in the sun.
The same, because the same sun falls on both. (A fair guess. The test will show.)

flow.context: This step of Dark Cloth, Pale Cloth is for guessing. You guess which tumbler of water will be warmer after 30 minutes in sunlight, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Leave the tumblers in the sun for 30 minutes. Do not move them. 2. While you wait, lay your hand on a dark thing and a pale thing that are already in the sun. Try a dark and a pale tile, or two parked scooters. 3. Use the rest of the time to ask your child again which tumbler they think will be warmer.
flow.say: While we wait, let's feel things that are already in the sun. Find one dark thing and one pale thing. Which is hotter to touch?
flow.kid: Leave the tumblers for 30 minutes. Find a dark thing and a pale thing in the sun. Touch each one quickly. Which is hotter?
flow.parent: Metal in strong sun can be hot enough to hurt, so touch it first yourself. You need not stand by the tumblers for the whole 30 minutes.
flow.wait: Leave the tumblers in the sun for 30 minutes.
flow.context: This step of Dark Cloth, Pale Cloth is the wait. Two wrapped tumblers of water stand in sunlight for 30 minutes, while you feel other dark and pale things in the sun.

flow.do: 1. After 30 minutes, ask your child to dip a finger of each hand into the two tumblers at the same moment. 2. If you have a thermometer, measure the black one, then the white one. 3. Write the results in the table. 4. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 5. Ask how this result fits the Daisy Planet rules.
flow.say: Which water is warmer? What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Dip a finger in each tumbler at the same time. Then tell your grown-up what you guessed, what you saw and why.

ask.q: Why did the water in the black cloth get warmer?
good: Black cloth takes in more of the sunlight and turns it into heat.
White cloth reflects more of the sunlight away.

ask.q: How does this fit the Daisy Planet rules?
good: Dark daisies take in more sunlight, so they warm the ground.
Pale daisies reflect sunlight, so they cool the ground.

flow.parent: In strong sun the black tumbler is usually 3 to 8 degrees warmer, which fingers can feel easily. If the sky was hazy and you feel no difference, leave them for another 30 minutes. On a cloudy day, wait for a sunny one. An LED lamp gives too little heat for this test.

check.q: Black cloth and white cloth lie in the same sunlight. Why does the black cloth get hotter?
options: Black cloth takes in more of the light
White cloth lets the heat pass through
The Sun shines more on black things
check.why: A black surface takes in most of the light that falls on it, and the light becomes heat. A white surface reflects most of the light away. The Sun shines equally on both.

flow.context: This is the last step of Dark Cloth, Pale Cloth. Two tumblers of water, one in black cloth and one in white, have stood in sunlight for 30 minutes. Here you compare them.

experiments.title: The Balancing Stick: what does a steady system need?
experiments.context: A system stays steady through balancing feedback: it notices a change and works against it. In this experiment you are the system. You balance a stick upright on your palm in three ways, and time how long the stick stays up.
experiments.question: You balance a stick upright on your palm. Does the stick stay up longer when you watch the top of the stick, when you watch your hand, or when your eyes are closed?
experiments.predict: Guess first. In which of the three ways will the stick stay up longest: watching the top, watching your hand, or eyes closed? In which will it fall soonest? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same stick, the same hand and the same spot in the room every time. Start every try the same way, with the stick held upright and then let go. Do 3 tries of each way, because one try can be a fluke. Change only where your eyes look.

materials.item: a straight stick about 60 centimetres to 1 metre long, such as a broom handle, a long ruler or a sheet of newspaper rolled tightly and taped
a clock or phone that shows seconds
a clear space about 2 metres wide, away from glass and lamps

experiments.safety: Do this in a clear space, away from windows, lamps and other people's faces. With eyes closed, stand still and let the stick fall.

schedule.what: Guess. Balance a stick on your palm in three ways, 3 tries each. Find the middle value for each way and explain the result.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with 9 times. Circle the middle value for each way. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how long the stick stayed up

data.label: At the top of the stick

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child standing in a clear room with a long stick balanced upright on an open palm, eyes looking up at the top of the stick.
setup.caption: 1. Balance the stick upright on your palm. Watch the top of the stick.

setup.art: The same child balancing the stick while looking down at the palm.
setup.caption: 2. Try again, watching only your hand.

setup.art: The same child with eyes closed, the stick starting to tip, and a grown-up beside them holding a phone timer.
setup.caption: 3. Try again with eyes closed. Time every try.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space. 2. Show how to stand the stick upright on a flat palm, hold it with the other hand, and then let go. 3. Let your child practise for two minutes, looking wherever they like. 4. Ask what their hand does when the stick starts to tip.
flow.say: Stand the stick on your palm and let go. Keep it up for as long as you can.
flow.kid: Stand the stick on your flat palm. Let go with the other hand. Keep the stick up. Notice what your hand does when the stick tips.

ask.q: What does your hand do when the stick starts to tip?
good: My hand moves the same way as the tip, to get back under the stick.
I see the stick lean and I move to catch it.

flow.parent: A longer stick is easier, because it tips more slowly. If the stick falls at once, use a longer one.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Balancing Stick. Here you practise balancing a stick upright on your palm.
