flow.do: 1. Explain the three ways: watching the top of the stick, watching the hand, and eyes closed. 2. Ask which way will keep the stick up longest, which will be shortest, and why. 3. Write the guesses and the reason down.
flow.say: You will try three ways. Watch the top, watch your hand, or close your eyes. Which will keep the stick up longest? Which will be shortest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are three ways: watch the top, watch your hand, eyes closed. Which will be longest? Which will be shortest? Write your guesses and why.
flow.context: This step of the Balancing Stick is for guessing. You guess whether a stick balanced on your palm stays up longest when you watch its top, watch your hand, or close your eyes.

flow.do: 1. Your child balances the stick while watching the top. Time from letting go until the stick falls or is caught. 2. Do 3 tries and write each time. 3. Do 3 tries watching only the hand. 4. Do 3 tries with eyes closed. Stand close, and catch the stick if it falls towards anyone. 5. Stop any try at 30 seconds and write '30 or more'.
flow.say: Ready? Let go. I am timing. Keep your eyes where we agreed for the whole try.
flow.kid: Do 3 tries watching the top. Do 3 tries watching your hand. Do 3 tries with eyes closed. A grown-up times each try. Write down all 9 times.
flow.parent: Most children keep the stick up for 5 to 20 seconds watching the top, a few seconds watching the hand, and about 1 second with eyes closed. Times vary a lot from try to try, which is why there are three.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Balancing Stick. You balance a stick on your palm in three ways, watching the top, watching your hand and with eyes closed, and time 3 tries of each.

flow.do: 1. For each way, put the 3 times in order and circle the middle one. 2. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Ask what the hand needed in order to keep the stick up.
flow.say: Circle the middle time for each way. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why was closing your eyes so much harder?
flow.kid: Circle the middle time for each way. Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why closed eyes made it so hard.

ask.q: Why did the stick fall so quickly when your eyes were closed?
good: My hand could not tell which way the stick was tipping.
The news about the tip did not reach me, so I could not correct it.
I could only feel the tip when it was already too late.

ask.q: Why was watching the top better than watching the hand?
good: The top moves furthest, so I saw the tip earlier.
I got the news sooner, so my correction was in time.

flow.parent: Balancing feedback needs three things: a way to notice the change, a way to act against it, and enough speed. With eyes closed the first is nearly gone. Watching the hand, the news comes too late.

check.q: A stick balanced on your palm falls quickly when your eyes are closed. Why?
options: You cannot notice the tip in time
check.why: To work against a change, a system must first notice the change. With eyes closed, the news that the stick is tipping arrives too late. The stick and the hand are just as they were.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Balancing Stick. You have timed a stick balanced on your palm in three ways. Here you compare the times and explain them.

activities.title: Zoom Out: one living being at five levels
activities.context: In this activity you choose one living being you can see from your window. Then you zoom out, step by step, from that one being to the whole Earth, and fill five circles. You find out how much one small being depends on.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
a window, a balcony or a doorstep

activities.record: Keep the drawing of five circles. Beside each circle, write one thing your living being gets from that level.

setup.art: A child at a window pointing at a crow on a wire, with paper and pencil on the sill.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one living being you can see.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with five circles, one inside the next, the smallest with a crow drawn in it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw five circles, one inside the next. Your being goes in the middle.

setup.art: The same five circles filled in: a crow, many crows, crows with trees and squirrels, the street with rain and soil, and the Earth.
setup.caption: 3. Fill each circle as you zoom out.

flow.do: 1. Look out together and choose one living being. A crow, a pigeon, an ant, a street tree or a potted tulsi will do. 2. Draw five circles on the paper, one inside the next. 3. Write your being's name in the smallest circle, and write ORGANISM beside it. 4. Ask what this one being needs in order to stay alive and have young.
flow.say: Choose one living being you can see. One living being on its own is called an organism.
flow.kid: Choose one living being outside. Draw five circles, one inside the next. Write its name in the middle. Write ORGANISM.

ask.q: What does this one organism need to stay alive and have young?
good: Food, water and air.
A place to rest or nest.
A mate of the same kind.

flow.parent: If nothing is in sight, your child can choose themself. A person is an organism too.
flow.context: This is the first step of Zoom Out. Here you choose one living being you can see, and draw them at the centre of five circles.

flow.do: 1. In the second circle, write how many of the same kind you can see, and write POPULATION. 2. In the third circle, name four other kinds of living being from the same place, and write COMMUNITY. 3. In the fourth circle, name four non-living things from the same place, and write ECOSYSTEM. 4. In the biggest circle, write EARTH, and write BIOSPHERE. Words are enough. Draw a little only if you want to.
flow.say: Now zoom out. Who else of the same kind lives here? Which other kinds of living being live here? What non-living things are here? The last circle is every living place on the Earth.
flow.kid: Circle 2: how many of the same kind. Write POPULATION. Circle 3: name four other kinds. Write COMMUNITY. Circle 4: name four non-living things. Write ECOSYSTEM. Circle 5: the Earth. Write BIOSPHERE.
flow.parent: Non-living things are water, air, soil, rock, sunlight and warmth. Remind your child that a community includes plants and beings too small to see.
flow.context: This step of Zoom Out fills in the levels. Around one living being you draw their population, their community, their ecosystem and the biosphere.

flow.do: 1. Point to each circle in turn. 2. Ask what your being gets from that level. 3. Write one thing beside each circle. 4. Ask which circle your being could do without.
flow.say: What does your being get from each circle? Is there any circle your being could do without?
flow.kid: Point to each circle. Tell what your being gets from it. Write one thing beside it.

ask.q: What does a crow get from each level?
good: From the population: a mate, and others to warn of danger.
From the community: food, and a tree to nest in.
From the ecosystem: water, air and warmth.
From the biosphere: rain and oxygen that come from far away.

check.q: All the house crows of one town, taken together, are which level of life?
check.why: A population is all the members of one species in one place. A community would include the other species of the town too. An ecosystem would also include the water, air and soil.

flow.context: This is the last step of Zoom Out. You have drawn one living being inside five circles. Here you say what that being gets from each level.

activities.title: Three Planets' Air: which planet is the odd one out?
activities.context: Venus, the Earth and Mars are neighbours, and all three are made of rock. In this activity you colour a strip for the air of each planet, and look for the odd one out. You will find out what is special about the air we breathe.

materials.item: squared paper, or plain paper and a ruler
colour pencils or crayons, in three colours

activities.record: Keep the three coloured strips. Under them, write one sentence saying which planet's air is the odd one out, and what makes it so.

setup.art: Three empty strips of 20 squares each, drawn one under the other and labelled Venus, Earth and Mars.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three strips of 20 squares. Each square stands for 5 parts in 100.

setup.art: The three strips coloured in: Venus and Mars almost all grey with one blue square, the Earth with 16 blue squares and 4 red squares.
setup.caption: 2. Colour each strip from the table of gases.

flow.do: 1. Say that Venus, the Earth and Mars are three rocky planets in a row, with the Earth in the middle. 2. Say that the air of Venus and the air of Mars are each about 95 parts carbon dioxide in every 100. 3. Ask what your child would expect the Earth's air to be, and why. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Venus is on one side of us and Mars is on the other. Their air is almost all carbon dioxide. So what would you expect the Earth's air to be made of? Why?
flow.kid: Venus and Mars have air that is nearly all carbon dioxide. The Earth is between them. Write your guess for our air, and why.

ask.q: What would you expect the Earth's air to be?
good: Mostly carbon dioxide too, because the Earth is between them. (A sensible guess from the pattern.)
Something different, because we can breathe it.

flow.context: This is the first step of Three Planets' Air. Here you guess what the Earth's air should be like, from the air of the two planets next to the Earth.

flow.do: 1. Draw three strips, each 20 squares long. Label them Venus, Earth and Mars. 2. Choose a colour for carbon dioxide, one for nitrogen and one for oxygen. 3. Venus: colour 19 squares as carbon dioxide and 1 as nitrogen. 4. Mars: colour 19 squares as carbon dioxide and 1 as nitrogen. 5. Earth: colour 16 squares as nitrogen and 4 as oxygen. 6. Beside the Earth's strip, make one tiny dot for carbon dioxide.
flow.say: Each square is 5 parts in every 100. Colour the three strips. The Earth's carbon dioxide is so little that it gets only a dot.
flow.kid: Draw three strips of 20 squares. Venus: 19 carbon dioxide, 1 nitrogen. Mars: the same. Earth: 16 nitrogen, 4 oxygen. Add one tiny dot of carbon dioxide for the Earth.
flow.parent: The measured figures are these. Venus: carbon dioxide about 96.5, nitrogen about 3.5. Mars: carbon dioxide about 95, nitrogen about 3, argon about 2, which we colour with the nitrogen. Earth: nitrogen 78, oxygen 21, argon about 1, carbon dioxide 0.04. The squares round these off.
flow.context: This step of Three Planets' Air is for colouring. You colour one strip of 20 squares for the air of Venus, one for the Earth and one for Mars.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three strips one under the other. 2. Ask which planet is the odd one out. 3. Remind your child that oxygen reacts easily: it rusts iron and it burns wood. 4. Ask why so much oxygen is surprising, and who could be making it.
flow.say: Which planet is the odd one out? Oxygen rusts iron and burns wood, so it keeps getting used up. Then why is there still so much oxygen in our air?
flow.kid: Which strip is the odd one out? Oxygen gets used up by rusting and burning.

ask.q: Why is there still so much oxygen in the Earth's air?
good: Plants and other green beings keep making it.
Someone must be putting it back all the time.
Venus and Mars have nobody to make it.

flow.parent: This is the reasoning James Lovelock and Dian Hitchcock used in the 1960s. A planet with no life has air in which nothing is left to react. The Earth's air is kept far from that state by living beings.

check.q: The Earth's air has far more oxygen than the air of Venus or Mars. What is the best explanation?
options: The Earth is the biggest planet
check.why: Photosynthesis by plants, seaweeds and bacteria gives out oxygen. Volcanoes give out carbon dioxide and water vapour, not oxygen. Volcanoes do add gases to the air, but oxygen is not one of them.

flow.context: This is the last step of Three Planets' Air. You have coloured strips for the air of Venus, the Earth and Mars. Here you find the odd one out and explain it.

activities.title: The Rice Heap: a property that only the whole has
activities.context: Each level of life has features that its parts do not have alone. These are called emergent properties. In this activity you find one in a heap of rice: its slope.

materials.item: uncooked rice
a sheet of newspaper
a ruler
a small tumbler to pour from

activities.record: Write the height and the width of both heaps, and the height divided by the width for each. Then write one sentence about what a heap has that a grain does not have.

setup.art: A hand pouring rice slowly from a steel tumbler onto a sheet of newspaper, where a small cone of rice is forming.
setup.caption: 1. Pour half a tumbler of rice slowly onto one spot.

setup.art: A ruler held upright beside a cone of rice to measure its height, with a second ruler lying across its base.
setup.caption: 2. Measure how high and how wide the heap is. Then pour a bigger heap and measure again.

flow.do: 1. Put one grain of rice on the newspaper. 2. Ask whether one grain has a slope. 3. Say that you will pour a small heap and then a heap twice as big. 4. Ask whether the big heap will be steeper, flatter or the same, and why.
flow.say: Look at one grain. Does one grain have a slope? Now think of a small heap and a big heap. Will the big heap be steeper, flatter or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at one grain of rice. Has it got a slope? You will pour a small heap and a big heap. Which will be steeper? Write your guess and why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rice Heap. Here you look at one grain of rice, and guess how the slopes of a small heap and a big heap will compare.

flow.do: 1. Pour half a tumbler of rice slowly onto one spot, from about 5 centimetres above the paper. 2. Measure the height of the heap and its width across the bottom. 3. Divide the height by the width. 4. Sweep the rice back and pour a full tumbler in the same way. 5. Measure and divide again.
flow.say: Pour slowly onto one spot. Now measure how high the heap is and how wide. Divide the height by the width. Let's see what the bigger heap gives.
flow.kid: Pour half a tumbler slowly onto one spot. Measure the height and the width. Divide height by width. Now pour a full tumbler. Measure and divide again.
flow.parent: Both heaps give nearly the same number, usually between 0.25 and 0.35. The big heap is higher and wider, but just as steep. If the heap slides flat, the paper is too smooth, so pour onto a cotton cloth.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Rice Heap. You pour a small heap and a big heap of rice, and compare how steep they are.

flow.do: 1. Ask where the slope is. Is it in any one grain? 2. Say that a feature of the whole that no part has is called an emergent property. 3. Ask for one emergent property of a population, one of a bee colony, and one of your child's own body.
flow.say: Both heaps had the same slope, but no grain has a slope. So where does the slope come from? Can you think of something a group of living beings has that one member does not have?
flow.kid: No grain has a slope, but every heap has one. Where does the slope come from?

ask.q: What does a group of living beings have that one member does not?
good: A population has a birth rate.
A bee colony keeps the hive warm.
A forest makes shade and damp air.
I can ride a cycle, but no single cell of my body can.

check.q: Which of these is an emergent property of a population of deer?
options: The number of fawns born each year
check.why: The number of births each year belongs to the whole population. No single deer has a birth rate. The other three are features of one deer.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Rice Heap. You found that heaps of rice have the same slope, though no grain has a slope. Here you look for the same idea in living beings.

activities.title: When the Daisies Run Out of Room: how far can a system steady itself?
activities.context: In the Daisy Planet Test, a paper planet of dark and pale daisies stayed near 26 degrees for many rounds while the Sun got hotter. By round 14 every square held a pale daisy. In this activity you play six more rounds, to see what happens next.

materials.item: the paper planet, the beans and the table from the Daisy Planet Test
a pencil

activities.record: Add rounds 15 to 20 to your table and to your graph. Write one sentence about what happened to the temperature, and why.

setup.art: The paper planet with all 20 squares covered by pale beans, and a notebook table beside it filled in to round 14.
setup.caption: 1. Start from round 14 of the Daisy Planet Test. All 20 squares hold pale daisies.

setup.art: The same paper planet with every square empty, and the pale beans swept to one side.
setup.caption: 2. Play six more rounds. Watch for the round when the daisies die.

flow.do: 1. Set out the planet as it was after round 14, with 20 pale daisies and no dark ones. 2. Add 6 rows to the table. The Sun numbers are 50, 53, 56, 59, 62 and 65. 3. Add one new rule: no daisy can live above 40 degrees. If the temperature goes above 40, take every daisy off. 4. Ask what will happen to the temperature now, and why.
flow.say: Every square is full of pale daisies, and the Sun is still getting hotter. There is one new rule. Above 40 degrees, all the daisies die. What do you think will happen in the next six rounds? Why?
flow.kid: Put 20 pale daisies on the planet. Add 6 rows to the table. New rule: above 40 degrees, all daisies die. What will happen now? Write your guess and why.
flow.parent: If you have not done the Daisy Planet Test, do that first. This activity needs its three rules.
flow.context: This is the first step of When the Daisies Run Out of Room. A paper planet is full of pale daisies and the Sun is still getting hotter. Here you guess what happens next.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds 15 to 20 with the same rules as before. 2. Write the temperature each round. 3. In the round when the temperature goes above 40, take off every daisy. 4. Add the six new points to the graph from the Daisy Planet Test.
flow.say: Work out the temperature. Can any more pale daisies grow? Is it above 40 yet?
flow.kid: Play rounds 15 to 20. Write the temperature each round. Above 40 degrees, take off all the daisies. Add the new points to your graph, or just read the numbers out.
flow.parent: The temperatures for rounds 15 to 20 are 30, 33, 36, 39, 42 and 65. The daisies die after round 19. In round 20 the planet is bare, so the temperature is the Sun number, 65.
flow.context: This is the main step of When the Daisies Run Out of Room. You play six more rounds of the paper Daisy Planet, with the Sun still getting hotter.

flow.do: 1. Look at the graph together. 2. Ask why the temperature began to climb in round 15. 3. Ask why it jumped by 23 degrees between rounds 19 and 20, when the Sun number rose by only 3.
flow.say: Why did the temperature start to climb after round 14? And why did it jump so far in the last round, when the Sun only got 3 degrees hotter?
flow.kid: Look at your graph. Find the round where the line starts to climb. Find the round where it jumps.

ask.q: Why did the temperature jump by 23 degrees in the last round?
good: The pale daisies had been cooling the planet by 20 degrees. When they died, that cooling was lost all at once.
Losing the daisies made the planet hotter, and a hotter planet cannot grow daisies.

flow.parent: A system that steadies itself can do so only up to a limit. Past the limit, the loss of the living beings makes the change worse. That is reinforcing feedback.

check.q: A paper planet is full of pale daisies and the Sun keeps getting hotter. What happens to the temperature?
options: It rises and falls in turn
check.why: With every square full, no more pale daisies can grow, so nothing is left to work against the hotter Sun. A balancing loop has a limit. Choosing 'level for ever' forgets that the daisies need room.

flow.context: This is the last step of When the Daisies Run Out of Room. You have played the paper Daisy Planet until the daisies died. Here you explain why the temperature jumped.

activities.title: The Gaia Council: six voices and three statements
activities.context: The Gaia hypothesis is the idea that living beings help keep the Earth fit for life. Scientists have argued about it for fifty years. In this activity you and a partner speak for two of those scientists. Then you sort three statements into what is agreed and what is still argued about.

materials.item: the explanation card called 'The Gaia hypothesis', which lists six voices
three slips of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Write the three statements in your notebook. Beside each, write 'agreed', 'argued about' or 'depends on what the word means', and one reason.

setup.art: A child and a parent sitting facing each other across a table, each holding a slip of paper with a scientist's name on it, a globe between them.
setup.caption: 1. Each of you chooses one voice from the Gaia card. Choose two who disagree.

setup.art: Three slips of paper being sorted into three piles labelled 'agreed', 'argued about' and 'depends on the word'.
setup.caption: 2. Sort three statements about the Earth into three piles.

flow.do: 1. Open the explanation card called 'The Gaia hypothesis'. 2. Read the six voices aloud, taking turns. 3. After each voice, ask your child to say the main point in one sentence of their own.
flow.say: Six scientists, or groups of scientists, speak on this card. After each one, tell me the main point in your own words.
flow.kid: Open the card called 'The Gaia hypothesis'. Read the six voices. After each one, say the main point in your own words.
flow.parent: The six are Lovelock and Margulis, Doolittle and Dawkins, Kirchner, Ward, Tyrrell, and the Earth system scientists. If six is too many for one sitting, read the first two and the last one.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Gaia Council. Here you read what six scientists, or groups of scientists, say about the Gaia hypothesis.

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses one voice to speak for. You choose a voice who disagrees. 2. Each of you speaks for 2 minutes, using evidence from this unit. 3. Each of you then asks the other one question. 4. Swap voices and do it again, more briefly.
flow.say: Choose a voice to speak for. I will take someone who disagrees. Use evidence: the three planets, the Daisy Planet, the frozen Earth. Afterwards we swap sides.
flow.kid: Choose one voice. Your partner takes a voice who disagrees. Speak for 2 minutes with evidence. Ask each other one question. Then swap sides.

ask.q: What evidence would make your scientist change their mind?
good: For Lovelock: finding that most feedback from life makes things less steady.
For Dawkins: a clear way that natural selection could favour beings who steady the planet.
For Tyrrell: finding other planets with life that also stayed steady for a very long time.

flow.parent: The aim is to state each side fairly, not to win. Swapping sides matters more than the first round.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Gaia Council. You and a partner each speak for a scientist in the argument about the Gaia hypothesis, and then swap sides.

flow.do: 1. Write these three statements on three slips. A: Living beings change the Earth's air, water and soil. B: Living beings keep the Earth steady and fit for life. C: The Earth is alive. 2. Ask your child to sort the slips into three piles: agreed, argued about, and depends on what a word means. 3. Ask for a reason for each.
flow.say: Here are three statements. Which one do almost all scientists agree with? Which one do they argue about? And which one depends on what a word means?
flow.kid: Write the three statements on slips. Sort them into three piles: agreed, argued about, depends on a word. Give a reason for each.

ask.q: Where does each statement go, and why?
good: A is agreed. The oxygen in the air is the clearest evidence.
B is argued about. The Earth froze over, and life has caused disasters too.
C depends on what 'alive' means. The Earth keeps steady but has no young.

check.q: Which statement do almost all scientists agree with?
options: The Earth is a living being
Life always keeps the Earth steady
Living beings change the Earth's air, water and soil
The Earth plans for the good of life
check.why: That living beings change the planet is well measured, and oxygen is the clearest case. Whether those changes keep the Earth steady is still argued about. Whether the Earth is 'alive' depends on what the word means.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Gaia Council. Here you sort three statements about the Earth into what is agreed, what is argued about, and what depends on the meaning of a word.

activities.title: One Change, Five Levels: follow a change up and down
activities.context: A change at one level of life passes to the other levels. In this activity you make a ladder of the five levels from paper slips. You follow one change down the ladder and another up it, to see how far each one reaches.

materials.item: a sheet of paper, torn into five slips for each ladder
a pencil and one colour pencil

activities.record: Keep the five slips. On the front of each, write what changed in the rain story. On the back, write what changed in the fig tree story.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a ladder of five wide rungs, labelled from the bottom: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biosphere.
setup.caption: 1. Lay five paper slips as a ladder, one for each level.

setup.art: The same ladder with a short note written on each rung and arrows pointing downward from the top rung.
setup.caption: 2. Start a change on one rung. Say what happens on each of the other rungs.

flow.do: 1. Write the five levels on five paper slips: organism, population, community, ecosystem and biosphere. Lay them in a column as a ladder, organism at the bottom. 2. Start at the top. Write on the top rung: the monsoon wind brings very little rain one year. 3. Think of a village tank (a pond) where egrets nest. Egrets are white water birds who eat fish and frogs. 4. Ask what happens on each rung below, one at a time, and write the answers.
flow.say: The rain comes from far away, so it belongs to the top rung. One year very little rain comes. What happens to the tank? Then to the beings who live there? Then to the egrets? Then to one egret chick?
flow.kid: Lay the five slips as a ladder, organism at the bottom. Top rung: little rain this year. Say what happens on each rung below. Write a few words on its slip.

ask.q: What happens on each rung when little rain comes?
good: Ecosystem: the tank shrinks and the mud dries.
Community: there are fewer fish, frogs and water plants.
Population: fewer egrets nest, and fewer chicks are raised.
Organism: one egret chick gets less food.

flow.context: This is the first step of One Change, Five Levels. Here you draw a ladder of the five levels of life, and follow a year of poor rain down from the top.

flow.do: 1. Turn the five slips over and lay them as a second ladder. 2. Start at the bottom. Write on the bottom rung: one big wild fig tree in a forest is cut down. 3. Say that fig trees fruit when few other trees do. Hornbills, macaques and bats all eat the figs and carry the seeds. 4. Ask what happens on each rung above, and write the answers. 5. Ask how far up the ladder this change reaches.
flow.say: Now start at the bottom. One big fig tree is cut. Who was eating those figs? What happens to them? What happens to the seeds they used to carry? Does this change reach the top rung?
flow.kid: Turn the slips over for a second ladder. Bottom rung: one big fig tree is cut. Say what happens on each rung above. Write a few words on the back of its slip.

ask.q: How far up does the loss of one fig tree reach?
good: Population: there is one fig tree fewer, and their fig wasps have nowhere to breed.
Community: hornbills, macaques and bats lose food in the lean months.
Ecosystem: fewer seeds are carried, so fewer young trees grow.
Biosphere: one tree is too small a change to notice.

flow.parent: One tree does not change the biosphere. A change at the bottom reaches the top only when a very great number of organisms do the same thing for a long time.
flow.context: This step of One Change, Five Levels goes upward. You follow the loss of one fig tree from the bottom rung of the ladder towards the top.

flow.do: 1. Ask what would have to be true for a change at the bottom rung to reach the top. 2. Give two real cases. Bacteria filled the air with oxygen. People burning coal, oil and gas are adding carbon dioxide to the air. 3. Ask what the two cases have in common.
flow.say: One tree did not change the whole Earth. But bacteria once did, and people are doing so now. What do those two cases have in common?
flow.kid: One tree did not change the Earth. Bacteria once did. People are doing it now.

ask.q: What do the bacteria and the people have in common?
good: There were a very great number of them, all doing the same thing.
They went on doing it for a long time.
What they gave out spread through the air of the whole Earth.

check.q: When can a change made by single organisms reach the whole biosphere?
options: When very many do the same for long
check.why: Cyanobacteria are tiny, but countless numbers of them gave out oxygen for millions of years. Size is not what counts. Humans are the second known case, not the only one.

flow.context: This is the last step of One Change, Five Levels. You have followed one change down the levels of life and one change up. Here you ask when a change at the bottom can reach the top.

projects.title: A World in a Jar: a sealed ecosystem for three weeks
projects.context: In this three-week project you build a tiny ecosystem in a glass jar and seal the lid. After that, only light goes in and only heat comes out. You watch what the water, the plant and the soil do. You find out how living things can reuse the same air and water again and again.

materials.item: a clear glass jar with a tight lid, about 1 litre, such as an old pickle or coffee jar
small pebbles or broken bits of clay pot
soil from a plant pot or a garden
a small plant with roots: a money plant cutting with two leaves, a clump of moss from a damp wall, or a small weed from a pot
water
a kitchen scale, if you have one
a marker pen or a strip of paper tape

projects.safety: A glass jar can break if it falls, so keep it on a low, steady shelf. Wash your hands after touching soil.

schedule.what: Build the jar: pebbles, soil, plant and water. Seal the lid. Weigh the jar if you can. Guess what you will see.
Look for mist and drops on the glass. If the glass is running wet all over, open the jar for an hour and seal it again.
Look at the glass in the morning and in the afternoon. Note when it is misty.
Draw the jar. Look for new growth, yellow leaves, mould or tiny animals.
Draw the jar again. Compare the drawing with day 7.
Weigh the jar again. Say what went round inside the jar and what crossed the glass.

projects.record: Keep a jar diary. On each day in the plan, write the date, where the water drops are, how the plant looks, and anything new. Write the weight on day 1 and day 21.

setup.art: A glass jar in layers: pebbles at the bottom, dark soil above, and a small two-leaved plant set in the soil.
setup.caption: 1. Put in pebbles, then soil, then the plant. Add 3 tablespoons of water.

setup.art: A hand screwing the lid on the jar, with a strip of tape across the lid and a date written on it.
setup.caption: 2. Seal the lid and write the date. Do not open the jar again.

setup.art: The sealed jar on a bright shelf away from direct sun, with mist and water drops on the inside of the glass.
setup.caption: 3. Keep the jar in bright light, out of direct sun. Watch the glass.

flow.do: 1. Put a layer of pebbles 2 centimetres deep in the jar. 2. Add soil until the jar is about one third full. 3. Make a hole with a finger, set the plant's roots in, and press the soil round them. 4. Sprinkle 3 tablespoons of water on the soil. The soil should be damp, not muddy. 5. Wipe the inside of the glass, screw the lid on tightly and write the date on it. 6. Weigh the jar if you have a scale, and write the weight. 7. Ask what will happen to the water, the plant and the weight in three weeks, and why.
flow.say: Once the lid is on, nothing goes in or out except light and heat. What do you think will happen to the water? To the plant? Will the jar get lighter, heavier or stay the same? Why?
flow.kid: Put in pebbles, then soil. Plant the plant. Add 3 tablespoons of water. Seal the lid and write the date. Weigh the jar. Guess what will happen to the water, the plant and the weight.

ask.q: Will the jar's weight change in three weeks? Why?
good: It will get lighter, because the plant drinks the water. (A fair guess. The scale will show.)
It will stay the same, because nothing can get out.

flow.parent: Put the jar where it gets bright light but no direct sun, for example a metre back from a window. Direct sun can heat a closed jar enough to kill the plant.
flow.context: This is day 1 of A World in a Jar. Here you build a small ecosystem of soil, water and one plant in a glass jar, and seal the lid.

flow.do: 1. Look at the inside of the glass. 2. Ask where the drops came from. 3. If the glass is running wet all over, there is too much water. Open the lid for one hour, then seal it again. This is the only time the jar may be opened.
flow.say: There is water on the glass. We did not put any there. Where do you think it came from?
flow.kid: Look at the glass. Are there mist and drops? Where did that water come from? Write your idea in the jar diary.

ask.q: Where did the drops on the glass come from?
good: From the damp soil. The water evaporated and then turned back into drops on the cool glass.
From the leaves. Plants give out water vapour.

flow.context: This is day 2 of A World in a Jar. A small plant and damp soil have been sealed in a glass jar for one day. Here you look for water on the glass.

flow.do: 1. On day 4, look at the jar in the morning and again in the afternoon. Note when the glass is misty and when it is clear. 2. On day 7, take a photo of the jar, or draw it. 3. Look for new leaves, yellow leaves, white threads of mould or tiny animals. 4. Write each one in the jar diary. Do not open the jar.
flow.say: When is the glass misty, and when is it clear? What is the water doing all day? Is anyone living in the jar that we did not put there?
flow.kid: On day 4, look in the morning and the afternoon. When is the glass misty? On day 7, photograph or draw the jar. Look for new leaves, mould or tiny animals.
flow.parent: Mist usually forms when the glass is cooler than the air inside, often at night and in the morning. Mould and tiny soil animals are part of the jar's community. If a leaf dies, leave it there, because decomposers will break it down.
flow.wait: Come back on day 4 and on day 7.
flow.context: This is the first week of A World in a Jar. A small ecosystem is sealed in a glass jar. Here you note when the glass is misty, and draw what is living inside.

flow.do: 1. On day 14, take another photo of the jar, or draw it again. 2. Lay it beside the day 7 photo or drawing. 3. Ask what has changed and what has stayed the same. 4. Ask where the plant is getting carbon dioxide from, now that the jar is sealed.
flow.say: Compare the two pictures. The plant needs carbon dioxide to make food. The lid has been shut for two weeks. So where is the carbon dioxide coming from?
flow.kid: Photograph or draw the jar again. Compare it with day 7. What has changed?

ask.q: Where does the plant's carbon dioxide come from in a sealed jar?
good: From the microbes in the soil, who breathe it out.
From the plant too, because plants respire as well as photosynthesise.
From dead leaves as decomposers break them down.

flow.context: This is day 14 of A World in a Jar. A plant has lived in a sealed glass jar for two weeks. Here you draw the jar and ask where the plant's carbon dioxide comes from.

flow.do: 1. On day 21, weigh the jar again and compare with day 1. 2. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why. 3. Ask your child to trace the water's path round the jar with a finger: up from the soil, onto the glass, down again. 4. Ask them to point to where light goes in and where heat goes out. 5. Ask how the jar is like the Earth, and how it is different.
flow.say: The weight is the same as on day 1. What does that tell us? What went round and round inside? What crossed the glass? How is this jar like the whole Earth?
flow.kid: Weigh the jar again. Has the weight changed? Trace the water's path round the jar with your finger. Point to where light goes in and where heat goes out.

ask.q: How is the sealed jar like the Earth, and how is it different?
good: Like: nothing is added, and the same water and air go round. Only light and heat cross.
Different: the Earth has millions of kinds of living beings, seas and winds.
Different: the jar is tiny, so one mistake can spoil it quickly.

flow.parent: The weight should be the same to within a gram or two, because no matter can cross glass. If the plant has died, the jar is still an ecosystem of microbes and mould, and the water still goes round. You can keep the jar sealed for months.

check.q: A sealed jar with soil, water and a plant weighs the same after three weeks. What does this show?
options: No matter went in or out
check.why: Plenty happened inside: water went round and the plant made food. But matter cannot cross glass, so the total stays the same. Light has no weight that a kitchen scale can measure.

flow.context: This is day 21 of A World in a Jar. A small ecosystem has been sealed in a glass jar for three weeks. Here you weigh the jar again and compare it with the Earth.

challenges.title: The Faster Sun: tune the Daisy Planet
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Daisy Planet Test, a paper planet of dark and pale daisies stayed steady while the Sun number rose by 3 each round. Here the Sun number rises by 5 each round, and you change one rule to help the planet keep up.
challenges.problem: The Sun number starts at 8 and rises by 5 every round for 12 rounds. Keep the Daisy Planet between 18 and 28 degrees for as many of the 12 rounds as you can.
constraints: The planet has 20 squares, and the rules are those of the Daisy Planet Test.
You may change one number only: how many daisies are added and taken off each round. It may be any number from 1 to 6.
Above 40 degrees, all the daisies die.
materials: the paper planet and the beans from the Daisy Planet Test
general: Raise the number from 3 to 4, so the daisies answer the Sun a little faster.
creative: Match the daisies to the Sun: if the Sun rises by 5, try changing 5 daisies each round.
Give the planet more ground. Draw 30 squares instead of 20, and see how many more rounds the daisies can hold.
Use two numbers: a big change when the temperature is far outside 20 to 25, and a small change when it is just outside.
challenges.your_turn: Now choose your own number and one more change of your own. Run all 12 rounds. How many rounds were between 18 and 28 degrees? What does your planet show about a living system facing a fast change?

setup.art: A notebook table with Sun numbers 8, 13, 18 and so on down the page, beside the paper planet and bowls of beans.
setup.caption: 1. Write the new Sun numbers: 8, 13, 18, up to 63.

setup.art: A child moving five pale beans onto the paper planet at once.
setup.caption: 2. Choose how many daisies change each round. Run 12 rounds and count the rounds between 18 and 28.

flow.do: 1. Write the 12 Sun numbers: 8, 13, 18, 23, 28, 33, 38, 43, 48, 53, 58 and 63. 2. Run the planet with the old number, 3 daisies a round. 3. Count the rounds in which the temperature is from 18 to 28.
flow.say: The Sun is rising faster now. Let's see how the old rule copes. Count the rounds that land between 18 and 28.
flow.kid: Write the Sun numbers: 8, 13, 18, up to 63. Run 12 rounds, changing 3 daisies each round. Count the rounds from 18 to 28 degrees.
flow.parent: With 3 daisies a round the temperatures are 8, 16, 24, 29, 28, 27, 29, 31, 33, 35, 38 and 43. Only 3 rounds are in range. The daisies cannot keep up.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Faster Sun. Here you run the paper Daisy Planet with a Sun that rises by 5 each round, to get the score to beat.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to choose a new number from 1 to 6, and to say why. The number is how many daisies to swap each round. The old rule swaps 3. 2. Run all 12 rounds with that number and count the rounds in range. 3. Try one more number and compare.
flow.say: Which number do you want to try? Why that one?
flow.kid: Choose how many daisies to swap each round, from 1 to 6. Say why. Run 12 rounds and count the rounds in range. Then try one more number.

ask.q: Is the biggest number the best?
good: No. With 6 the planet swings too far each time.
The best number is close to the Sun's own step.

flow.parent: The scores out of 12 are these. With 1 daisy a round: 2. With 2: 3. With 3: 3. With 4: 4. With 5: 8. With 6: 6. Five wins because it matches the Sun's step of 5. Six is too much, so the temperature swings above and below.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Faster Sun. You choose how many daisies change each round on the paper Daisy Planet, and test your choice over 12 rounds.

flow.do: 1. Compare the scores. 2. Ask why a number that is too small fails, and why a number that is too big also does worse. 3. Ask what this says about real living beings when their surroundings change fast.
flow.say: Too slow failed, and too fast was not the best either. Why? What does this tell us about real forests and seas when the climate changes quickly?
flow.kid: Compare your scores. Why did a small number fail? Why was 6 not the best? What does this say about real forests?

ask.q: What does the Faster Sun show about living systems?
good: They can steady a slow change, but they fall behind a fast one.
A forest takes many years to grow, so it cannot answer a change that takes only a few.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Faster Sun. You have tested several rules on the paper Daisy Planet under a fast-rising Sun. Here you explain which worked best.

challenges.title: A Sealed Home: close every loop
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. Between 1991 and 1993, eight people lived sealed inside a glass building called Biosphere 2, and their oxygen ran low. Here you design a sealed home for one person, in which every waste becomes something that someone else needs.
challenges.problem: Design a sealed home in which one person can live for a year. Nothing goes in or out except light and heat. Show where the person's oxygen, water and food come from, and where every waste goes.
constraints: No arrow may end in 'thrown away'. Every waste must go to someone or something that uses it.
Count everyone who breathes, including the beings in the soil.
Use only living beings and simple machines that really exist.
materials: a large sheet of paper, or two sheets taped together
general: Grow plants. They take in the person's carbon dioxide and give out oxygen and food.
Catch the water that plants and people give out as vapour. Let it turn back into drops on a cool surface, as in a sealed jar.
Compost food scraps and toilet waste, and return the compost to the plant beds.
creative: Add tanks of tiny green algae. They make oxygen in little space, and some kinds can be eaten. The European Space Agency tests this in a project called MELiSSA.
Grow mushrooms on the stems and leaves that people cannot eat.
Keep fish who eat plant scraps, and use the water from their tank to feed the plants.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw your own sealed home. Follow one drop of water all the way round, and then one carbon atom. Does each one get back to where it started? Who did you forget to count?

setup.art: A sheet of paper with one person drawn in the middle, three arrows pointing in labelled oxygen, water and food, and three arrows pointing out labelled carbon dioxide, waste water and waste.
setup.caption: 1. Draw one person. Draw what they need coming in and what they give out.

setup.art: The same drawing with plants, a water collector and a compost bin added, and every arrow joined into loops.
setup.caption: 2. Add living beings and machines until every arrow joins a loop.

flow.do: 1. Draw one person in the middle of the sheet. 2. Draw three arrows going in: oxygen, water and food. 3. Draw arrows going out: carbon dioxide, water in breath, sweat and urine, and solid waste. 4. Ask what would happen in a sealed room with only this person in it.
flow.say: Here is one person in a sealed home. What do they take in? What do they give out? What would happen if the room held nothing else?
flow.kid: Draw one person. Draw arrows in for oxygen, water and food. Draw arrows out for carbon dioxide, water and waste. Or tell your grown-up what goes in and out.

ask.q: What happens to one person alone in a sealed room?
good: The oxygen runs down and the carbon dioxide builds up.
The food and water run out, and the waste piles up.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Sealed Home. Here you draw what one person takes in and gives out, before designing a sealed home around them.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to add living beings and machines, one at a time. 2. For each one, draw what goes in and what comes out. 3. Join each waste arrow to someone who needs it. 4. Go on until no arrow ends in nothing.
flow.say: Who could use the carbon dioxide? Where could clean water come from? What could be done with the waste? Keep going until every arrow joins up.
flow.kid: Add plants, animals or machines, one at a time. Draw what each takes in and gives out. Join every waste arrow to someone who needs it.
flow.parent: Let your child's design be their own. If they are stuck, read out one idea from the lists above. The most forgotten beings are the microbes in the soil, who take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.
flow.context: This is the main step of A Sealed Home. You add living beings and machines to a drawing of a sealed home, until every waste goes to someone who needs it.

flow.do: 1. Follow one drop of water round the drawing with a finger. 2. Follow one carbon atom round. 3. Tell the story of Biosphere 2: the soil microbes used oxygen faster than the plants made it. 4. Ask whether the design has counted the soil.
flow.say: Follow a drop of water all the way round. Now a carbon atom. In Biosphere 2, the builders forgot how much the soil microbes breathe. Did we count ours?
flow.kid: Follow one drop of water round your drawing. Follow one carbon atom. Does each get back to the start? Did you count the microbes in the soil?

ask.q: Why is a sealed home so much harder to run than the whole Earth?
good: It is small, so a small mistake changes the air quickly.
The Earth has millions of kinds of living beings, and a home has only a few.
The Earth's air and sea are huge, so changes are slow.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Sealed Home. You have drawn a sealed home for one person. Here you test the drawing by following water and carbon all the way round.

items.p: A temple tank holds fish, frogs, water plants, water and mud. Which level of life is the whole tank?
items.why: An ecosystem is the living beings of a place together with the water, mud, air and sunlight. Choosing 'community' leaves out the non-living things.

items.p: All the members of one species who live in one place are called a ____.
items.why: A population is one species in one place, such as all the house sparrows of Mysuru.

items.p: Match each level of life to an example.
items.why: Each level contains the one before. A strong answer can give a second example of each from a place the child knows.
pairs: all the neem trees of a village
all the living beings of the village
the village's living beings with its soil, water and air
every living place on the Earth

items.p: True or false: a community includes the water and the soil of a place.
items.why: False. A community is only the living beings. When the water, soil, air and sunlight are counted too, the level is an ecosystem.

items.p: Sort these parts of a pond ecosystem.
items.why: Frogs, fungi, bacteria and moss are living beings. Mud, sunlight, water and air are not alive, but every living being in the pond needs them.

items.p: A forest gets its monsoon rain from winds that crossed the sea. Which level supplies that rain?
items.why: The wet wind comes from far outside the forest, so no level inside the forest can supply it. An ecosystem depends on the biosphere for its rain and its air.

items.p: In the Daisy Planet Test, the bare planet reached 47 degrees. Explain why the planet with daisies stayed near 26.
items.a: Whenever the planet went above 25 degrees, three pale daisies replaced three dark ones. Pale daisies reflect sunlight, so each one cooled the planet by a degree. That cancelled the extra heat from the Sun.
items.why: A strong answer says that the daisies changed the temperature and the temperature changed the daisies. It uses numbers from the test.

items.p: A feature that a whole has, and that no part has alone, is called an ____ property.
items.why: The slope of a rice heap and the birth rate of a population are emergent properties.

items.p: Three of these are non-living parts of an ecosystem. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Soil microbes are living beings, so they belong to the community. Water, sunlight and rock are non-living.

items.p: True or false: balancing feedback works against a change.
items.why: True. Balancing feedback brings things back towards where they were, as sweat brings your body's heat down.

items.p: Which gas is about one fifth of the Earth's air, and was made by living beings?
items.why: Oxygen is 21 parts in every 100 of the air, and nearly all of it came from photosynthesis. Nitrogen is the biggest part of the air, at 78 in 100.

items.p: Draw one living being from near your home inside five circles. Label the five levels.
items.a: Five circles, one inside the next. From the centre: one organism, their population, their community, their ecosystem with water and soil, and the Earth as the biosphere.
items.why: A strong drawing adds something new in each circle. The ecosystem circle must show at least one non-living thing.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: Put these in order, from the smallest level to the biggest.
a: All the lions of the Gir forest
All the living beings of the Gir forest
The Gir forest with its soil, streams and air
Every living place on the Earth
items.why: The order is organism, population, community, ecosystem, biosphere. Each one contains the one before.
items: All the living beings of the Gir forest
Every living place on the Earth
The Gir forest with its soil, streams and air
All the lions of the Gir forest

items.p: Label each loop 'balancing' or 'reinforcing'. Loop A: hot, sweat, cooler. Loop B: ice melts, dark sea warms, more ice melts.
items.why: In loop A the result works against the change. In loop B the result adds to the change.
items.art: Two circles of arrows. Circle A joins a hot face, a drop of sweat and a cool face. Circle B joins melting ice, dark water and a sun.

items.p: Is a population a real thing, or only a word? Two friends disagree.
items.a: A strong answer uses the rice heap. The slope is real and can be measured, yet no grain has one. In the same way a birth rate is real, yet no single crow has one. It also grants the other side its point: a population is made of nothing but crows.
items.why: Both views hold something true. The parts are all there is, and yet the whole has features the parts lack.

views.says: Only single crows are real. 'Population' is just a short word for a lot of crows.
A population is real. It has a birth rate, and no single crow has a birth rate.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use the rice heap as evidence. Then say one thing the other friend has right.

worksheets.title: How living beings change the Earth (stretch)

items.p: Very old rocks hold minerals that oxygen destroys. Younger rocks do not. What does this show?
opts: The early air had almost no oxygen
The early Earth had no rocks
items.why: Those minerals could only last in air without oxygen. So the air changed, about 2,400 million years ago, when bacteria had made enough oxygen.

items.p: Rusting and burning keep using up oxygen. Explain how the air can still be one fifth oxygen.
items.a: Plants, seaweeds and tiny cells in the sea give out oxygen when they photosynthesise. They keep putting oxygen back as fast as rusting, burning and breathing take it away.
items.why: A strong answer says that oxygen is being made all the time, not that it was made once and stayed.

items.p: True or false: the Amazon rainforest adds most of the oxygen to the Earth's air.
items.why: False. The living beings of the forest use up almost all the oxygen the forest makes. The forest matters for rain, for carbon and for the beings who live there.

items.p: A year of poor rain reaches a village tank. Match each change to the level where it happens.
items.why: A change at the top passes down through every level. A strong answer could trace a second change upward.
pairs: The monsoon wind brings little rain
The tank dries to cracked mud
Fish, frogs and water plants all become fewer

items.p: The share of sunlight that a surface reflects is called its ____.
items.why: Snow has a high albedo, because it reflects most of the light. Dark sea has a low albedo.

items.p: A black car and a white car stand in the same sun. Which gets hotter inside, and why?
opts: Black: it takes in more light
The same: the sun is the same
items.why: A dark surface takes in more of the light, and that light becomes heat. Reflecting light keeps the white car cooler, not hotter.

items.p: Put this loop in order, starting with 'The air warms'.
a: The water takes in more sunlight
items.why: After the last step, the air warms again, so the loop goes round and grows. This is reinforcing feedback.
items: The water takes in more sunlight

items.p: Sort these loops into balancing and reinforcing.
items.why: In a balancing loop the result works against the change. In a reinforcing loop the result adds to it, so the change grows.
items: A pressure cooker's whistle lets out steam when the pressure rises
Each person who hears a rumour tells two more
You are thirsty, you drink, and the thirst goes
A rolling snowball picks up more snow as it grows
The pupils of your eyes shrink in bright light
Money in a bank earns interest, and the interest earns interest

items.p: Daisy Planet: the Sun number is 32, with 2 dark and 9 pale daisies. What is the temperature? What happens next?
items.a: 32 + 2 - 9 = 25 degrees. That is inside the range from 20 to 25, so no daisies are added or taken off this round.
items.why: A strong answer shows the sum, and then uses the rules to say what the daisies do.

items.p: Draw a balancing loop from your own day, with arrows. Mark where the change is pushed back.
items.a: A loop of at least three steps that returns to its start, such as: I feel hungry, I eat, my stomach is full, I stop eating. The step that works against the change is marked.
items.why: A strong drawing goes all the way round, and shows which step pushes back.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: The Daisy Planet filled up with pale daisies. Why did its temperature then start to rise?
opts: There was no room for more pale daisies
items.why: Each new pale daisy had cancelled one degree of extra heat. With every square full, nothing was left to work against the hotter Sun.

items.p: True or false: if a model works, the real world must work the same way.
items.why: False. A model shows what could happen under its own rules. Whether the real world follows those rules has to be tested in the real world.

items.p: Three of these are emergent properties. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A wing length belongs to one bee. The other three belong only to a whole made of many parts.

items.p: A sealed jar with a plant weighs the same after three weeks. What crossed the glass, and what did not?
items.a: Light went in and heat came out. No water, air or soil crossed the glass, so the weight stayed the same. Inside, the water went round and round.
items.why: A strong answer separates energy, which crosses the glass, from matter, which does not.

items.p: Does life keep the Earth fit for life? Two scientists disagree.
items.a: A strong answer for the first view uses the long record of liquid water under a brightening Sun, or the Daisy Planet. A strong answer for the second uses the frozen Earth, or the point that a daisy planet was built so that each daisy's needs match the planet's. It then says what the other side has right.
items.why: This is a real argument among scientists. Both sides accept that life changes the planet. They differ on whether those changes steady it.

views.says: Living beings and the Earth form one system. Its balancing loops have kept the planet fit for life for a very long time.
Natural selection helps an organism and their family. Nothing makes living beings work for the good of a planet.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with more? Give one piece of evidence. Then say one thing the other scientist has right.

items.p: One scientist says our steady Earth may be luck. Explain his point by imagining 100 planets with life.
items.a: Suppose life starts on 100 planets and only a few happen to stay fit for life. Beings who can ask questions will only ever be found on those few. They will all see a long steady record, even if luck alone made it.
items.why: A strong answer sees that we could not be looking from a planet where things went badly. So our own steady record is weak evidence.

items.p: Astronomers find a far planet whose air holds oxygen and methane together. Why is that exciting?
opts: Something must keep making both gases
Those gases make the planet blue
items.why: Oxygen and methane react with each other. If both are there, something must be making them all the time. On the Earth, living beings do that.

items.p: In the Faster Sun, changing 6 daisies a round did worse than changing 5. Suggest why.
items.a: With 6, each correction was bigger than the change it was correcting. The temperature went past the comfortable range on the other side, and then had to be corrected back. With 5, the correction matched the Sun's step.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of overshooting: correcting by more than the change.

items.p: True or false: living beings have always made the Earth better for other living beings.
items.why: False. When bacteria first filled the air with oxygen, that oxygen was a poison to most living beings of the time. Life changes the Earth, sometimes for the worse.

items.p: Put this slow loop in order, starting with 'The Earth warms'.
a: More rain falls and rock wears away faster
Wearing rock takes carbon dioxide out of the air
items.why: This is a balancing loop that takes about a million years. Roots and fungi make the rock wear away faster, so living beings take part in it.
items: Wearing rock takes carbon dioxide out of the air
More rain falls and rock wears away faster

items.p: The young Sun was about a quarter dimmer, yet the early seas stayed liquid. What is the likeliest reason?
opts: The early air trapped more heat
The Earth was nearer the Sun
items.why: Most scientists think the early air held more heat-trapping gases, such as carbon dioxide and methane. Exactly how much of each is still being worked out.

items.p: A graph from the Daisy Planet Test has two lines. Label the bare planet's line and the daisy planet's line.
a: The straight, steep line: the bare planet
The line that climbs and then runs level: the daisy planet
items.why: The bare planet follows the Sun number, which rises by 3 every round. The daisy planet levels off near 26 degrees.
items.art: A graph with rounds 1 to 14 along the bottom and temperature up the side, one straight steep line and one line that climbs and then runs level, each with an empty label box.

items.p: Keeping conditions inside steady while conditions outside change is called ____.
items.why: Your body does this with its warmth, and a honeybee colony does it with the warmth of the hive.

items.p: Sort each statement: agreed by almost all scientists, or still argued about.
items.why: That life changes the Earth is well measured. Whether those changes keep the Earth steady, and whether the Earth is 'alive', are still argued about.
items: Living beings made most of the oxygen in the air
Forests return water to the air
Life keeps the Earth's temperature steady
The Earth has both kinds of feedback loop
Life's changes to the Earth mostly help life

items.p: Is the Earth alive? Three people disagree.
items.a: A strong answer says which signs of life it is counting. It uses evidence such as the steady record, the lack of young, or the recycling of waste. It then answers one of the other views fairly.
items.why: The disagreement is partly about the Earth and partly about what the word 'alive' should mean. A strong answer notices both.

views.says: Yes. The Earth takes in energy and keeps itself steady, as a living body does.
No. A living being has parents and young. The Earth has neither.
Neither. The Earth is a huge set of ecosystems. It recycles all its waste, which no organism does.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Say which signs of life you are counting. Then answer one of the others.

items.p: Bacteria changed the air with oxygen. People are changing it with carbon dioxide. Give one likeness and one difference.
items.a: Likeness: in both cases a very great number of organisms gave out the same gas for a long time, and it spread through the whole air. Difference: the bacteria took many millions of years, and people have taken about two hundred. People also know what they are doing and can choose to change it.
items.why: A strong answer compares the scale and the speed, and notices that only one of the two can know and choose.

items.p: Draw the Earth with one arrow for energy coming in, one for energy going out, and a loop for matter.
items.a: The Earth with a sunlight arrow coming in, a heat arrow going out, and a closed loop on the surface, for example water or carbon going round.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that energy passes through, while matter stays and is used again.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: In the sealed building Biosphere 2, oxygen fell though there were many plants. What had the builders not counted?
items.why: The rich soil held huge numbers of microbes, who used oxygen faster than the plants made it. Every being who breathes has to be counted.

items.p: The Earth is 12,700 km across. Nearly all life is in a layer 20 km thick. What fraction is that?
items.why: 12,700 divided by 20 is 635. So the layer is about one six-hundredth of the Earth's width.

items.p: Three of these are evidence that life changes the Earth. Which is not?
opts: Soil made from rock and dead leaves
Rain returned to the air by forests
The Earth's distance from the Sun
items.why: The Earth's distance from the Sun has nothing to do with living beings. The other three were made by living beings.

quiz.p: All the species living in one mangrove, without the water or the mud, are which level?
quiz.why: Many species in one place are a community. Add the water and the mud, and the level is an ecosystem.

quiz.p: Which level counts the living beings of a place and the non-living things together?
quiz.why: An ecosystem is a community with the water, air, soil and sunlight around them.

quiz.p: A lone tigress lives in a forest with plenty of prey and water. What can she not do alone?
quiz.why: To have cubs she needs a mate, so she needs a population. This is one way an organism depends on the next level up.

quiz.p: True or false: a change made by tiny organisms can never reach the whole biosphere.
quiz.why: False. Cyanobacteria are too small to see, yet they filled the Earth's air with oxygen. It took a very great number of them and a very long time.

quiz.p: Which of these belongs to a honeybee colony, but not to one bee?
opts: Keeping the hive at a steady warmth
quiz.why: Thousands of bees shivering and fanning together hold the hive near 35 degrees Celsius. One bee cannot do that. It is an emergent property.

quiz.p: A loop makes a small change grow bigger and bigger. What is it called?
quiz.why: Reinforcing feedback adds to a change. Balancing feedback works against a change, and homeostasis is the steadiness it produces.

quiz.p: Wild dogs eat deer. When deer increase, the dogs increase and eat more deer. What kind of loop is this?
quiz.why: More deer leads to more dogs, and more dogs brings the deer down again. The result works against the change.

quiz.p: Mars has almost no oxygen in its air. What is the best reason?
opts: Oxygen is too heavy for Mars
Mars has no air at all
quiz.why: Oxygen reacts with rocks and is used up unless something keeps making it. On the Earth, living beings do that. Mars does have air, and most of it is carbon dioxide.

quiz.p: On the Daisy Planet, what cools the planet when it gets too hot?
opts: Pale daisies spread and reflect sunlight
quiz.why: Above 25 degrees, pale daisies replace dark ones. Pale daisies reflect sunlight, so the planet cools. The model has no rain.

quiz.p: True or false: the Daisy Planet can stay steady however hot the Sun gets.
quiz.why: False. When every square is full of pale daisies, no more cooling can be added. A balancing loop works only up to a limit.

quiz.p: Which of these is a real criticism of the Gaia hypothesis?
opts: The Earth is too big to study
Natural selection cannot make beings serve a planet
quiz.why: Natural selection favours what helps an organism and their family. Critics ask how it could ever favour what helps a whole planet.

videos.why: Jane Poynter was one of the eight people sealed inside Biosphere 2. She tells what happened when the oxygen fell. The first 8 minutes are enough.
videos.check: Id, title and channel confirmed through YouTube's public lookup. Not watched from here: a parent should preview it. It is a talk for adults.

videos.title: The tiny creature that secretly powers the planet | Penny Chisholm
videos.why: Penny Chisholm tells how her team found Prochlorococcus, the tiny sea cells who do a large share of the Earth's photosynthesis.
videos.check: Id, title and channel confirmed through YouTube's public lookup. Not watched from here: a parent should preview it. It is a talk for adults, so watch it together and pause often.

applications: Astronomers look for life on planets around other stars by studying the air of those planets. They look for gases that would vanish unless something kept making them.
People who work to protect the forests of the Western Ghats point to the rain those forests send on to farms in Tamil Nadu.
Engineers who plan homes on the Moon or Mars must close every loop of air, water and waste. Biosphere 2 showed how hard that is.
Climate scientists use computer models of the whole Earth, with air, sea, ice and living beings all acting on each other. The Daisy Planet is a very small relative of those models.
Doctors use the idea of balancing feedback to understand how the body holds its warmth and its blood sugar steady.
In 1987, the countries of the world agreed to stop making the gases that were destroying ozone in the upper air. That agreement treated the atmosphere as one system shared by all.
Farmers who grow many crops together, with trees and ponds, are looking after a whole community and ecosystem, and not just one population of one crop.

spotted.text: A crow on a wire is an organism. The flock gathering at dusk on one big tree is part of a population.
spotted.art: A big rain tree at dusk with dozens of crows settling on the branches.

spotted.text: A temple tank or a village pond is an ecosystem you can walk round in five minutes.
spotted.art: A stone-stepped temple tank with lotus leaves, fish near the steps and an egret on the edge.

spotted.text: Mist rising from a forested hill after rain, in Munnar, Coorg or Cherrapunji, is water that the trees are sending back to the air.
spotted.art: A green hill range with white mist lifting off the treetops after rain.

spotted.text: A black umbrella in the sun gets hot to touch. A white cotton veshti or dupatta stays cooler. That is albedo.
spotted.art: A black umbrella and a white cotton cloth lying side by side in bright sun.

spotted.text: A pressure cooker's whistle lifts when the pressure is high and drops when it falls. That is balancing feedback in the kitchen.
spotted.art: A pressure cooker on a stove with steam hissing from its whistle.

spotted.text: A steaming compost heap or a warm heap of cut grass shows that the microbes inside are respiring.
spotted.art: A compost heap on a cool morning with thin steam rising from the top.

spotted.text: A termite mound by a roadside in Telangana or Karnataka is built and cooled by a whole colony. No single termite could build one.
spotted.art: A tall red termite mound beside a dry road, with tiny termites at one opening.

spotted.text: The green layer on a pond or an old tank in summer is made of algae and cyanobacteria. The ancestors of cyanobacteria were the first makers of the oxygen in the air.
spotted.art: A pond with a bright green layer on the water near the bank.

open_questions.q: Do living beings, taken all together, make the Earth's climate steadier or less steady?
open_questions.why_open: Life is part of balancing loops and of reinforcing loops. Nobody has yet added them all up for the whole Earth.

open_questions.q: Did the Earth stay fit for life through a steadying system, or partly through luck?
open_questions.why_open: We have only one planet with life to study. A fair test needs other planets with life, and none has been found yet.

open_questions.q: How do the tiny beings of the sea affect the clouds above them?
open_questions.why_open: In 1987, four scientists proposed that gases from phytoplankton help clouds to form and so cool the sea. Later measurements suggest the effect is weaker and more tangled than they thought.

open_questions.q: How much of the rain over land was given out by plants somewhere else?
open_questions.why_open: It can only be worked out with computer models and special measurements of water, and the answers differ from region to region.

open_questions.q: Can people build a small sealed world that keeps going for many years?
open_questions.why_open: Biosphere 2 needed oxygen from outside. Smaller tests have kept people alive for months, but always with some help from machines and stores.

ask_kids: Which living beings made the oxygen in the breath you just took?
Look at one bird. What is their population? What is their community?
What in this room would be different if nothing had ever lived on the Earth?
Where is there balancing feedback in our kitchen? In your body?
What can our whole family do that no one of us can do alone?
When it rains, how much of that water do you think came from trees?
Is our home a sealed jar? What comes in, and what goes out?
Would you call the Earth alive? What would make you change your mind?

jokes.j: Why were the pale daisies never worried about the Sun?
What did the grain of rice say to the heap?
jokes.a: 'I never knew I had a slope in me.' The heap said, 'You don't. We do.'

jokes.j: What is the biosphere's favourite party game?
jokes.a: Pass the parcel. Nothing ever gets thrown away.

jokes.j: Why is an ecosystem never lonely?
Why did the soil microbes lose at hide-and-seek?
jokes.a: There were crores of them, and every one was breathing.

jokes.j: What did the phytoplankton say to the tree?
jokes.a: 'Half of that oxygen is ours. You're welcome.'

jokes.j: Why is a thermostat such a good friend?
jokes.a: It always notices when things are getting too heated.

jokes.j: Why did the sealed jar never go on holiday?
jokes.a: Everything it needed kept coming round at home.

jokes.j: Why did the crow say, 'I contain multitudes'?
jokes.a: He had just learned he was an organism, in a population, in a community, in an ecosystem, in a biosphere.

maths.problem: On the Daisy Planet, the Sun number is 35. There are 9 pale daisies and no dark daisies. What is the temperature?
maths.explain: Start with the Sun number, 35. Add 1 for each dark daisy: there are none. Take away 1 for each pale daisy: 35 - 9 = 26. So the temperature is 26 degrees.
maths.context: This is about the Daisy Planet Test. On a paper planet, each dark daisy warms the planet by 1 degree and each pale daisy cools it by 1 degree.
maths.why_maths: The rule turns three numbers into one temperature. Working it out each round is how the model runs.

maths.problem: The bare planet was between 20 and 27 degrees in 3 rounds. The daisy planet was in that range in 12 rounds. How many times as many rounds is that?
maths.explain: Divide the daisy planet's rounds by the bare planet's rounds: 12 ÷ 3 = 4. So the planet with daisies stayed comfortable for 4 times as many rounds.
maths.context: This is about the Daisy Planet Test. A bare paper planet and a planet with daisies were both warmed by a Sun that got hotter each round.

chart.title: Rounds between 20 and 27 degrees, out of 14

maths.why_maths: Saying '4 times as long' tells you how big the daisies' effect was, not just that there was one.

maths.problem: From round 10 to round 13 the Sun number rose by 3 each round, and the temperature stayed at 26. How many pale daisies were added each round? Explain how you know.
maths.explain: Each pale daisy cools the planet by 1 degree. The Sun added 3 degrees each round. For the temperature to stay the same, the cooling must also grow by 3 degrees. So 3 pale daisies were added each round.
maths.context: This is about the Daisy Planet Test. On a paper planet, each pale daisy cools the planet by 1 degree, while the Sun number rises by 3 each round.
maths.why_maths: A level line on a graph means two changes are cancelling each other. Finding the missing number shows exactly what cancelled what.

maths.problem: The Earth is about 12,700 kilometres across. Nearly all life is in a layer about 20 kilometres thick. On a model Earth 1 metre across, how thick is that layer?
maths.explain: The model is 1 metre, which is 1,000 millimetres, for 12,700 kilometres. Divide 1,000 by 12,700 to find what 1 kilometre becomes: about 0.08 millimetres. Multiply by 20: 0.08 × 20 = 1.6 millimetres.
maths.context: This is about the biosphere, the part of the Earth where living beings are found. It reaches from the deepest sea to the highest-flying birds.
maths.why_maths: The numbers 20 and 12,700 are hard to picture together. A scale model turns them into sizes you can hold in your hands.

maths.problem: In Three Planets' Air, one square stands for 5 parts in 100. The Earth's carbon dioxide is 0.04 parts in 100. What fraction of one square is that?
maths.answer: 0.008 of a square, which is less than one hundredth of a square.
maths.explain: Divide the gas by the size of one square: 0.04 ÷ 5 = 0.008. One hundredth of a square would be 0.01, and 0.008 is smaller than that. So the carbon dioxide gets only a tiny dot.
maths.context: This is about Three Planets' Air. There you coloured strips of 20 squares to show the gases in the air of Venus, the Earth and Mars.
maths.why_maths: The same gas fills 19 squares on Venus and a dot on the Earth. Working out the size of the dot shows how different the two planets are.

maths.problem: In the Faster Sun, the scores were 3 rounds with 3 daisies, 4 with 4, 8 with 5 and 6 with 6. Do the scores fit the rule 'the bigger the number, the better'?
maths.answer: No. The score rises up to 5 daisies and then falls at 6.
maths.explain: Put the scores in order of the number of daisies: 3, 4, 8, 6. They rise from 3 to 4 to 8, but then drop to 6. So the best number is 5, in the middle, and not the biggest one.
maths.context: This is about the Faster Sun challenge. There the Sun number rose by 5 each round, and you chose how many daisies changed each round on the paper Daisy Planet.

chart.title: The Faster Sun: rounds between 18 and 28 degrees, out of 12

maths.why_maths: A pattern that rises and then falls is easy to miss in a list. Looking at all four scores together tests the rule before you trust it.

warmup.q: Name the five levels of life, from smallest to biggest.
What do you add to a community to make an ecosystem?
warmup.a: The non-living things around them: water, air, soil, rock and sunlight.

warmup.q: Which living beings made most of the oxygen in the air?
warmup.a: Plants, seaweeds, phytoplankton and bacteria, through photosynthesis.
A feature a whole has that none of its parts has alone, such as the slope of a rice heap.

warmup.q: Which kind of feedback keeps things steady?
warmup.a: Balancing feedback, which works against a change.

warmup.q: Which gets hotter in the sun, a dark cloth or a pale cloth?
warmup.a: The dark cloth, because it takes in more of the light.

warmup.q: What does the Gaia hypothesis say?
warmup.a: That living beings and the non-living Earth form one system that keeps the Earth fit for life.

warmup.q: Give one reason some scientists doubt the Gaia hypothesis.
warmup.a: Natural selection cannot make living beings work for a planet. Also, the Earth has frozen over in the past.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. Nothing was tried at home. The Daisy Planet Test (core, and in the short path) is a paper model with fixed rules, so it always gives the same numbers. I ran the rules on a computer: the daisy planet's temperatures for rounds 1 to 14 are 8, 14, 20, 23, 26, 23, 26, 23, 26, 26, 26, 26, 26 and 27, and the parent note lists them so a slip can be found. It needs 20 dark and 20 pale beans or buttons, and about 20 minutes of small sums. When the Daisies Run Out of Room and the Faster Sun use the same rules, and their numbers were also run on a computer. Dark Cloth, Pale Cloth needs direct sunlight for 30 minutes, so it is not in the short path. On a hazy day the difference can be too small to feel, and the step says to wait longer or try another day. The Balancing Stick needs a clear space and a stick of at least 60 centimetres, because a short ruler falls too fast to time. The Rice Heap gives a ratio of about 0.25 to 0.35, which is my estimate from the usual slope of poured rice and was not measured. A World in a Jar takes three weeks. A jar in direct sun overheats, and a jar with too much water stays fogged, so the steps say where to keep it and when it may be opened once. The plant may die, and the step says what to do then. The Gaia Council is hard for a nine-year-old alone, and works best with a parent. Facts checked online on 18 Nov 2026: the 1965, 1967, 1974 and 1983 papers, the critics and their years, the Amsterdam Declaration wording, the air of Venus, Mars and the Earth, the Great Oxidation Event at about 2,400 million years, the young Sun at about three quarters of today's light, the Western Ghats rain study, the Sahara dust figure, Prochlorococcus, the bee nest temperature, the word 'biosphere' in 1875, and the Atharva Veda, Marcus Aurelius and Thirukkural passages. Biosphere 2's lowest oxygen is given as 'about 14 in 100' because sources say 14.2 or 14.5. The dates of the frozen Earth were checked too. Not checked online, and written from general knowledge: the 1987 ozone agreement, Lovelock's instrument, Kirchner's exact years, the MELiSSA project and the height bar-headed geese fly. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel, but nobody has watched them yet, and two are talks for adults.
